cards: A change in a person's behaviour or opinions as a result of real or imagined pressure from a person or group.
A deep type of conformity: the person genuinely accepts the group's norms. Change is both public and private and lasts even when the group is absent.
A superficial, temporary type of conformity: the person publicly goes along with the majority but privately disagrees. It stops when group pressure is removed.
Conforming because we want to be right. In new or ambiguous situations we look to others who we think know better. A cognitive process that usually leads to internalisation.
Conforming because we want to be liked and accepted, and fear rejection. An emotional process that usually leads to compliance.
Lucas et al. (2006): students conformed more to wrong answers on difficult maths problems than on easy ones. People conform when unsure, as ISI predicts.
Asch's interviews: some participants said they conformed because they felt self-conscious and feared disapproval. When answers were written privately, conformity fell (to about 12.5%).
123 American male students judged which of three comparison lines matched a standard line. One naive participant sat with 6-8 confederates who gave the same wrong answer on 12 of 18 critical trials.
Participants conformed on 36.8% of critical trials. 25% never conformed and 75% conformed at least once. In the control condition the error rate was under 1%.
Conformity rose with the size of the majority up to about 3 confederates (31.8%). Adding more made little further difference. With 1 confederate it was about 3%.

When one confederate gave the correct answer (or a different wrong answer), conformity fell to about a quarter of its usual level (5.5% with a truthful dissenter). Breaking unanimity frees the participant.
When the lines were made more similar in length (harder task), conformity increased. ISI matters more when the situation is ambiguous.
Perrin and Spencer (1980) repeated the study with UK engineering students and found just 1 conforming trial out of 396. The original result may reflect conformist 1950s (McCarthy-era) America.
Participants knew they were in a study (demand characteristics), the task was trivial with no consequences and the groups were strangers, so findings may not generalise to real life.
Only American men were tested, so findings may not apply to women or collectivist cultures (Smith & Bond 1998 found higher conformity there). Participants were deceived and may have been embarrassed.
A form of social influence where a person follows a direct order from someone they see as an authority figure, who usually has the power to punish disobedience.

40 male volunteers acted as 'teacher' and were told to give increasing shocks (15V to 450V) to a 'learner' (a confederate) for wrong answers. The experimenter used four standard prods, ending with 'You have no other choice, you must go on'.

All 40 went to at least 300V and 65% (26 of 40) went to the full 450V. Many showed extreme tension: sweating, trembling, nervous laughter, and three had seizures. Students had predicted only about 3% would go to 450V.
A mental state where we feel no personal responsibility for our actions because we believe we are acting for an authority figure, as their agent. The opposite is the autonomous state.
The shift from the autonomous state to the agentic state. It happens when we see someone as a legitimate authority above us in a social hierarchy.
Features of a situation that let a person ignore or minimise the harm they are doing, reducing their moral strain. For example, blaming the victim or denying the damage.

We obey people higher in a social hierarchy because society agrees their authority is legitimate. We learn this in childhood from parents and teachers. Some authority is destructive, used to order harmful behaviour.
Blass and Schmitt (2001) showed students a film of Milgram's study. They blamed the experimenter rather than the participant, and recognised his legitimate 'scientific' authority.

It does not explain why 35% of Milgram's participants refused, or why 16 of 18 nurses in Rank and Jacobson (1977) refused to give an overdose. Mandel (1998) notes Reserve Police Battalion 101 killed civilians without direct orders.
Kilham and Mann (1974) found only 16% of Australian women went to the top voltage, while Mantell (1971) found 85% of German participants did. Different cultures view authority differently.
Teacher and learner in the same room: obedience fell from 65% to 40%. Touch proximity (forcing the learner's hand onto a plate): 30%. Experimenter giving orders by phone: 20.5%.
When the study moved from Yale University to a run-down office block in Bridgeport, obedience fell to 47.5%. Yale's prestige gave the experimenter more legitimacy.
When the experimenter in a grey lab coat was replaced by an 'ordinary member of the public' in everyday clothes, obedience fell to 20%.

A field experiment in New York. Confederates in a jacket and tie, a milkman's outfit or a security guard's uniform gave orders to passers-by. People were about twice as likely to obey the 'guard' as the man in the jacket and tie. Supports uniform.

Supported by Bickman's field study. Miranda et al. (1981) found over 90% obedience in Spanish students, so findings generalise across cultures. But Orne and Holland (1968) argued participants may have seen through the set-up, especially in the uniform variation.

Adorno et al. (1950): a personality type prone to obedience. Features: exaggerated respect for authority, contempt for people of lower status, conventional attitudes, rigid black-and-white thinking and prejudice. Measured by the F-scale.
Harsh, strict parenting with conditional love and criticism. Hostility towards the parents cannot be expressed, so it is displaced onto weaker others (scapegoats). A psychodynamic explanation.

Support: Elms and Milgram (1966) found fully obedient participants scored higher on the F-scale. Limitations: it cannot explain obedience across whole societies (e.g. Nazi Germany); the research is correlational; the F-scale has acquiescence bias and only measures right-wing authoritarianism.

Others who resist pressure help a person to resist. In conformity, a dissenter breaks unanimity (Asch: 5.5%). In obedience, a disobedient peer acts as a model (Milgram: obedience fell to 10% with two disobedient confederates).

Allen and Levine (1971): conformity fell with a dissenter even when he wore thick glasses and clearly could not see. Gamson et al. (1982): 29 of 33 groups rebelled against an oil company's unjust demands.

Rotter (1966). Internals believe events result from their own behaviour, so they resist social influence more. Externals believe events are due to luck, fate or others, so they conform and obey more. LOC is a continuum.

Support: Holland (1967) found 37% of internals refused to go to the highest shock compared with 23% of externals. Against: Twenge et al. (2004) found Americans became more external over 40 years yet also more resistant to obedience.
When a minority persuades others to adopt their beliefs or behaviour. It usually leads to internalisation, with public and private change.
The minority must be consistent: synchronic (all members say the same thing) and diachronic (they say the same thing over time). This makes the majority rethink their views.
Taking part in activities at personal cost or risk shows commitment. The augmentation principle: the majority pays more attention when the minority makes sacrifices.
Nemeth (1986): rigid repetition can seem dogmatic, so the minority should balance consistency with flexibility and accept reasonable counter-arguments.

Over time more people switch from the majority to the minority position and the rate of conversion speeds up, until the minority becomes the majority. This is the snowball effect described by Moscovici.

Groups of 6 (2 confederates) judged the colour of 36 blue slides. A consistent minority calling them 'green' got agreement on 8.42% of trials; an inconsistent minority on 1.25%; the control group 0.25%.

Support: Martin et al. (2003) found people who heard a minority message were less likely to change their view again later, suggesting deeper processing. Limitations: artificial tasks such as slide colours lack real-world relevance, and effects in research are small (about 8%).

Atkinson and Shiffrin (1968): memory is three separate unitary stores: sensory register, short-term memory and long-term memory. Attention moves information from the SR to STM, maintenance rehearsal moves it from STM to LTM, and retrieval brings it back to STM.
Coding: modality-specific (iconic for visual, echoic for sound). Capacity: very large. Duration: under half a second (iconic).
Coding: mainly acoustic (Baddeley 1966). Capacity: 7 ± 2 items (Miller 1956), or about 4 chunks (Cowan 2001). Duration: about 18 to 30 seconds without rehearsal (Peterson & Peterson 1959).
Coding: mainly semantic (Baddeley 1966). Capacity: potentially unlimited. Duration: potentially a lifetime (Bahrick et al. 1975).

Participants recalled lists of acoustically or semantically similar and dissimilar words. Immediate recall (STM) was worse for acoustically similar words; recall after 20 minutes (LTM) was worse for semantically similar words.
Measured digit span to test STM capacity. Mean span was 9.3 digits and 7.3 letters.
24 students recalled consonant trigrams after counting backwards in threes for 3 to 18 seconds (to stop rehearsal). Recall was about 80% after 3 seconds and about 10% after 18 seconds.
392 American graduates matched names to yearbook photos. Recall was about 90% within 15 years of graduating and about 70% after 48 years, showing LTM can last a very long time.
Grouping items into larger meaningful units to increase the capacity of STM (Miller 1956).
Case studies such as HM and Clive Wearing: hippocampal damage stopped new LTMs forming while STM stayed intact, suggesting separate stores. Baddeley's research shows STM and LTM code differently.

STM is not unitary: KF (Shallice & Warrington 1970) had poor verbal STM but normal visual STM. LTM is not unitary either. Rehearsal is not the only route into LTM (Craik & Watkins 1973). Much of the research used artificial materials.
Baddeley and Hitch (1974): a model of STM made of a central executive that controls slave systems: the phonological loop, the visuo-spatial sketchpad and (added in 2000) the episodic buffer.
Supervises the system and allocates attention and resources to the slave systems. It has very limited capacity and does not store information.

Deals with auditory information and keeps its order. The phonological store holds words you hear (inner ear); the articulatory process allows maintenance rehearsal (inner voice). Capacity is about 2 seconds of speech.
Stores visual and spatial information (inner eye). Capacity about 3 to 4 objects. Logie (1995) divided it into the visual cache (form and colour) and the inner scribe (spatial arrangement).
Added in 2000. A temporary store that integrates visual, spatial and verbal information from the other stores and links to LTM, keeping a sense of time sequence. Capacity about 4 chunks.
People remember lists of short words better than lists of long words, supporting a phonological loop capacity of about 2 seconds of speech (Baddeley et al. 1975).

Baddeley et al. (1975): doing two visual tasks at once was harder than doing a visual and a verbal task together. Two visual tasks compete for the visuo-spatial sketchpad, supporting separate slave systems.

Strengths: KF had impaired verbal but intact visual STM, supporting separate components; dual-task studies support it. Limitations: the central executive is vague and poorly defined; evidence from brain-damaged patients may not generalise.
Forgetting occurs because two pieces of information conflict, causing one or both to be forgotten or distorted. It mainly explains forgetting in LTM and is worse when the memories are similar.
An older memory disrupts a newer one. Example: a teacher who has learned many names in the past struggles to remember the names of a new class.
A newer memory disrupts an older one. Example: learning a new phone number makes it harder to recall the old one.
Participants learned a word list then a second list. Recall of the first list was worst when the second list was synonyms, showing interference is strongest when material is similar.
Baddeley and Hitch (1977): rugby players who had played more games over the season forgot more names of teams they had played. This is retroactive interference in a real setting.

Many studies used artificial word lists. Tulving and Psotka (1971) found interference effects disappeared when cues were given, so interference may block access temporarily rather than erase memories.

Forgetting because the cues present when we learned are absent when we try to recall (encoding specificity principle, Tulving 1983). Context-dependent forgetting involves external cues; state-dependent forgetting involves internal cues.
Divers learned words on land or underwater and recalled them in the same or the other setting. Recall was about 40% lower when the environments did not match. Context-dependent forgetting.
Participants took antihistamines (causing drowsiness). Recall was worse when their internal state at recall did not match their state at learning. State-dependent forgetting.

Strong research support with real uses (e.g. the cognitive interview). But Baddeley argued contexts must be very different (land vs underwater) for strong effects, and Godden and Baddeley (1980) found no context effect when memory was tested by recognition.
The ability of people to remember details of events, such as crimes or accidents, that they have seen. Accuracy can be affected by leading questions, post-event discussion and anxiety.
45 students watched film clips of car crashes and were asked 'About how fast were the cars going when they ___ each other?'. 'Smashed' gave a mean estimate of 40.5 mph; 'contacted' gave 31.8 mph.

A week later, participants who heard 'smashed' were more likely to report seeing broken glass (16 of 50) than those who heard 'hit' (7 of 50) or the control group (6 of 50), though there was none. Supports the substitution explanation.
Response bias: the wording of the question does not change the memory, it only influences the answer chosen. Substitution: the wording changes the memory itself.

When co-witnesses discuss an event, their memories can become contaminated as they combine information (memory conformity). Gabbert et al. (2003): 71% of witnesses who discussed a crime reported details they had not seen.

Johnson and Scott (1976): participants who saw a man holding a bloody knife identified him correctly 33% of the time, compared with 49% for those who saw a man holding a greasy pen. Attention narrows onto the weapon.
Yuille and Cutshall (1986): 13 witnesses to a real shooting in Canada gave accurate accounts 4 to 5 months later. Those who reported the highest stress were the most accurate (about 88% vs 75%).
Deffenbacher (1983) applied the Yerkes-Dodson law to EWT: recall improves as anxiety rises up to an optimal point, then falls sharply.

Lab studies such as Loftus and Palmer lack realism; Foster et al. (1994) found real witnesses are more accurate because their answers have consequences. The research has real value for police questioning. Older witnesses may be less accurate (Anastasi & Rhodes 2006).
Fisher and Geiselman (1992): a police interviewing technique with four main parts: report everything, reinstate the context, reverse the order and change perspective.

Report everything: include trivial details as they may trigger other memories. Reinstate the context: mentally return to the scene, using context cues. Reverse the order: reduces reliance on schemas. Change perspective: describe events from another viewpoint.
Fisher et al. (1987) added: knowing when to make eye contact, reducing the witness's anxiety, minimising distractions, getting the witness to speak slowly and asking open-ended questions.

Köhnken et al. (1999) meta-analysis of 50+ studies: the enhanced CI produced 34% more correct information than a standard interview, but also more incorrect information. It is time-consuming and needs training, so police often use only parts of it.
A close, two-way emotional bond between two people, especially an infant and caregiver, shown by proximity seeking, separation distress and secure base behaviour.

Lorenz split a clutch of goose eggs: half hatched with the mother, half in an incubator where the first moving thing they saw was Lorenz. The incubator goslings followed Lorenz. This is imprinting, which happened within a critical period of a few hours.
Lorenz observed that birds that imprinted on humans later tried to court humans as adults.

Support: Regolin and Vallortigara (1995) found chicks imprinted on simple shapes. But birds' attachment differs from mammals' (more emotional), so generalising to humans is hard, and Guiton (1966) found imprinting effects on mating could be reversed.

16 rhesus monkeys were reared with two wire 'mothers', one giving milk and one covered in cloth. They cuddled the cloth mother and ran to it when frightened, whichever one gave milk. Contact comfort matters more than food.

Monkeys reared with wire mothers became aggressive and less sociable, bred less and some neglected, attacked or killed their offspring. There seemed to be a critical period of about 90 days for a real mother.

Real-world value: helps social workers understand risks in neglect and informs zoo breeding. Ethical issues: severe lasting harm to the monkeys. Monkeys are more similar to humans than geese, but generalisation is still debated.

Dollard and Miller (1950), 'cupboard love'. Classical conditioning: food (UCS) brings pleasure (UCR); the caregiver (NS) is paired with food and becomes a CS producing pleasure. Operant conditioning: crying is reinforced by the caregiver's response, and the caregiver is negatively reinforced when crying stops. Attachment is a secondary drive.

Against: Harlow's monkeys preferred comfort to food, and Schaffer and Emerson (1964) found many babies' main attachment was not to the person who fed them. It ignores interactional synchrony. Conditioning may still play some part.

Attachment is innate and adaptive because it improves survival. Babies have social releasers (crying, smiling, cuteness) that trigger care. Monotropy means one attachment, usually to the mother, is more important than the others. Includes a critical period and an internal working model.
Law of continuity and law of accumulated separation
Continuity: the more constant and predictable a child's care, the better the attachment. Accumulated separation: the effects of every separation add up, so 'the safest dose is a zero dose'.
About the first 2 years (sometimes given as up to 2.5 years). If an attachment has not formed by then, the child will find it much harder to form one later. Later described as a sensitive period.
A mental representation of the child's first attachment relationship. It acts as a template for future relationships and affects how the child will later parent.

Support for social releasers: Brazelton et al. (1975) found babies became distressed when their caregivers ignored their signals. Support for the IWM: Bailey et al. (2007) found mothers' attachment to their own mothers predicted their babies' attachment type. Against monotropy: Schaffer and Emerson found many babies form multiple attachments at the same time.

Ainsworth (1970): a controlled observation of 12-18 month olds in a novel room, with 8 episodes of about 3 minutes each. It measures proximity seeking, exploration and secure base behaviour, stranger anxiety, separation anxiety and reunion behaviour.
About 60 to 75% of British infants. They explore happily using the caregiver as a secure base, show moderate stranger and separation anxiety and are easily comforted on reunion.
About 20 to 25%. They explore freely but do not use the caregiver as a secure base, show little or no stranger or separation anxiety and little reaction on reunion.
About 3%. They explore less and seek more closeness, show strong stranger and separation anxiety and resist comfort on reunion.

Strengths: high inter-observer reliability (Bick et al. 2012: 94% agreement) and predictive validity (secure infants have better later outcomes). Limitations: it may be culture-bound (Takahashi 1990: Japanese infants rarely separated from mothers showed extreme distress), and it missed a fourth type, disorganised (Main & Solomon 1986).

A meta-analysis of 32 Strange Situation studies in 8 countries (1,990 children). Secure attachment was most common everywhere (75% in Britain, 50% in China). Insecure-resistant was least common overall. Variation within countries was 1.5 times greater than between countries.

The large combined sample improves validity. But the Strange Situation is an imposed etic based on American norms, and countries are not cultures: Van IJzendoorn and Sagi (2001) found differences between Tokyo and rural Japan. Simonelli et al. (2014) found 50% secure and 36% avoidant in Italy, possibly due to more working mothers.

Bowlby (1951): prolonged emotional separation from the mother during the critical period (first 2.5 years) causes lasting damage to intellectual and emotional development, such as low IQ and affectionless psychopathy (no guilt or empathy).

Of 44 teenage thieves, 14 were classed as affectionless psychopaths and 12 of those had experienced long separations from their mothers before age 2. Only 2 of a 44-person control group had such separations.

Bowlby did the interviews and diagnoses himself, so bias is possible. Lewis (1954) studied 500 young people and found early separation did not predict criminality. Rutter distinguished deprivation (losing an existing bond) from privation (never forming one). Koluchová's (1976) twins recovered from severe privation, so the critical period may be a sensitive period.
The effects of living in an institution such as an orphanage, where there is no consistent caregiver and little emotional care.
Rutter's English and Romanian Adoptees (ERA) study

Rutter et al. (2011) followed 165 Romanian orphans adopted into British families, compared with 52 British adoptees. Those adopted after 6 months showed disinhibited attachment and lower IQs (mean 77 if adopted after 2). Those adopted before 6 months showed no lasting difference (mean IQ about 102).

Zeanah et al. (2005): 95 children in Romanian institutions compared with 50 who had never been institutionalised. 74% of the controls were securely attached compared with 19% of the institutionalised group; 44% of the institutionalised group showed disinhibited attachment.

Disinhibited attachment (equally friendly to strangers and familiar people, attention-seeking), intellectual disability (lower IQ), and poor peer relationships. Effects may be reversed if children are adopted early, before about 6 months.

Real-world impact: better care in institutions, key workers and early adoption. Romanian orphanages were extreme, so results may not generalise to other institutions. Earlier studies had confounding variables (e.g. trauma), which the Romanian studies reduced.

Via the internal working model: secure attachment leads to better friendships and adult relationships; avoidant attachment links to difficulty with intimacy; resistant attachment links to jealousy and control. It also affects parenting (intergenerational continuity).

Kerns (1994): securely attached infants tend to form the best-quality childhood friendships. Myron-Wilson and Smith (1998): secure children were unlikely to be involved in bullying, insecure-avoidant children were most likely to be victims and insecure-resistant children most likely to be bullies.

A 'love quiz' in a US newspaper had 620 replies. 56% were secure, 25% avoidant and 19% resistant. Secure respondents had the longest relationships; avoidant respondents reported jealousy and fear of intimacy.
Early attachment and later relationships: evaluation

Mixed evidence: Zimmermann et al. (2000) found infant attachment type did not predict adolescent attachment. Studies like Hazan and Shaver rely on retrospective self-report. Findings are correlational, so other factors (parenting style, genes) may explain both. The theory can be deterministic.
Behaviour may be a sign of mental ill health if it is numerically rare. Example: an IQ below 70 (about 2% of people) is one criterion for intellectual disability.

Strength: useful in real-life assessment (e.g. scores on the Beck Depression Inventory). Limitations: some rare traits are desirable (IQ above 130), labelling someone abnormal can harm them, and not everyone with an unusual trait needs treatment.
Deviation from social or cultural norms

Behaviour may be a sign of mental ill health if it breaks the unwritten rules of a society or culture. Example: antisocial personality disorder involves failing to follow lawful and normal behaviour. Norms differ between cultures and over time.

Strength: used in diagnosing conditions such as antisocial personality disorder. Limitations: cultural relativism (hearing voices is normal in some cultures), and it has been used to justify abuses of human rights (e.g. the historical 'diagnosis' of drapetomania in enslaved people).

A person may have a mental health problem if they cannot cope with ordinary demands of life, such as hygiene, holding down a job or keeping relationships. Rosenhan and Seligman (1989) signs: not following interpersonal rules, severe personal distress, irrational or dangerous behaviour. Measured with scales such as the GAF.

Strength: it considers the patient's own experience of distress. Limitations: it is hard to separate failing to function from choosing an unusual lifestyle, and judging what counts as 'adequate' is subjective and culture-bound.

Jahoda (1958): mental ill health is not meeting the criteria for ideal mental health, such as having no symptoms or distress, a rational self-perception, self-actualisation, coping with stress, a realistic view of the world, good self-esteem, independence and success in work and love.
Deviation from ideal mental health: evaluation

Strength: a positive, comprehensive approach that focuses on what is needed for good mental health. Limitations: culture-bound (self-actualisation and independence are individualist Western values) and the standard is unrealistically high, since very few people meet every criterion.
An anxiety disorder involving an irrational, persistent fear of an object or situation. Types include specific phobias, social anxiety and agoraphobia.
Panic (crying, screaming, running away), avoidance (making an effort to avoid the phobic stimulus) and endurance (staying in its presence but with high anxiety).
Anxiety (long-lasting unpleasant arousal) and fear (an immediate, intense response). The emotional response is unreasonable and out of proportion to the danger.
Selective attention to the phobic stimulus (hard to look away), irrational beliefs about it, and cognitive distortions (e.g. a spider is perceived as bigger or more aggressive than it is).
A mood disorder characterised by low mood and low energy. Types include major depressive disorder and persistent depressive disorder.
Changed activity levels (lethargy, or sometimes agitation), disrupted sleep (insomnia or hypersomnia) and eating (more or less appetite), and aggression or self-harm.
Lowered mood (feeling worthless or empty), anger towards self or others, and lowered self-esteem (sometimes self-loathing).
Poor concentration, attending to and dwelling on the negative (and recalling unhappy events), and absolutist black-and-white thinking.
Obsessive-compulsive disorder: an anxiety disorder characterised by obsessions (persistent, intrusive thoughts) and/or compulsions (repetitive behaviours).
Compulsions are repetitive (e.g. hand-washing, counting, checking), compulsions reduce anxiety, and avoidance of situations that trigger anxiety.
Overwhelming anxiety and distress, accompanying depression (low mood), and guilt and disgust (e.g. over minor moral issues or dirt).
Obsessive thoughts (about 90% of patients have them), cognitive coping strategies (e.g. praying, meditating), and insight that the anxiety is excessive, while staying hypervigilant.
Mowrer (1960): the behavioural explanation of phobias. A phobia is acquired through classical conditioning and maintained through operant conditioning.

Classical conditioning: a neutral stimulus is paired with an unconditioned stimulus that causes fear, so the NS becomes a conditioned stimulus that triggers fear. Little Albert (Watson & Rayner 1920): a white rat paired with a loud noise led to fear of the rat, which generalised to similar furry objects.
Operant conditioning through negative reinforcement: avoiding the phobic stimulus removes the unpleasant anxiety, so avoidance is reinforced and repeated. This keeps the phobia going.

Strength: it led to exposure therapies (SD and flooding). Limitations: it ignores the cognitive side of phobias (irrational beliefs), cannot explain phobias that begin without a frightening experience, and does not explain biological preparedness (Seligman 1971): we readily fear things that were dangerous to our ancestors, such as snakes, but not cars.

A behavioural therapy (Wolpe 1958) that uses counterconditioning: the patient learns to associate the phobic stimulus with relaxation instead of fear. Based on reciprocal inhibition: you cannot be relaxed and afraid at the same time.

1) Anxiety hierarchy: patient and therapist list situations from least to most frightening. 2) Relaxation training: breathing exercises, muscle relaxation or meditation. 3) Exposure: the patient works up the hierarchy while relaxed, moving on only when calm at each level (in real life or imagined).

Effective: Gilroy et al. (2003) treated 42 spider phobics; the SD group was less fearful than a relaxation-only group at 3 and 33 months. Suitable for people who cannot use cognitive therapies (e.g. some with learning disabilities). Acceptable: patients prefer it to flooding and fewer refuse it.

Immediate exposure to the phobic stimulus at full intensity, without a hierarchy, in one long session (2 to 3 hours) until anxiety subsides. The patient cannot avoid it, so the fear response is extinguished because the feared outcome never happens.

Strength: cost-effective; it can work in one session and Ougrin (2011) found it as effective as other treatments and quicker. Limitations: very traumatic, so informed consent is vital and some patients quit, wasting time and money; less effective for complex phobias such as social phobia with strong cognitive aspects.
Beck (1967): depressed people have faulty information processing and negative self-schemas, and hold a negative triad of automatic thoughts about themselves, the world and the future.
Attending to the negatives of a situation and ignoring the positives, black-and-white thinking, overgeneralising and catastrophising.
Packages of negative information about ourselves, often formed in childhood, which make us interpret all information about ourselves negatively.

Support: Grazioli and Terry (2000) found pregnant women with high cognitive vulnerability were more likely to develop postnatal depression; Cohen et al. (2019) found early cognitive vulnerability in 473 adolescents predicted later depression. Real-world use in CBT and screening. Limitations: it cannot explain every feature (e.g. anger, or rare delusions such as Cotard syndrome) and the link may be correlational.

Ellis (1962): A is the activating event (a negative event), B is the belief about it (rational or irrational, e.g. 'musturbation', 'I-can't-stand-it-itis', utopianism), C is the consequence (rational beliefs lead to healthy emotions, irrational beliefs lead to depression).

It explains reactive depression (with an obvious trigger) but not depression that has no clear trigger. It led to REBT. But it can be seen as blaming the patient, since it focuses on beliefs rather than real circumstances such as poverty or abuse.

Assessment, then identifying and challenging negative or irrational thoughts. Beck's cognitive therapy treats the patient as a scientist who tests the reality of their beliefs, often through homework. Ellis's REBT extends ABC to ABCDE: D is disputing irrational beliefs and E is the effect.

Empirical argument (what is the evidence?), logical argument (does the belief follow from the facts?), pragmatic argument (is the belief useful?). Behavioural activation encourages enjoyable activities.

Effective: March et al. (2007) studied 327 depressed adolescents; after 36 weeks 81% improved with CBT, 81% with antidepressants and 86% with both. Limitations: it may not suit severe depression or people with low motivation; relapse is common (Ali et al. 2017: 42% relapsed within a year); it may neglect life circumstances; the therapist-client relationship may matter more than the technique.

OCD is polygenic: Taylor (2013) found up to 230 candidate genes. Examples: the SERT gene (serotonin transporter) and the COMT gene (regulates dopamine). It is aetiologically heterogeneous: different combinations of genes cause OCD in different people.

Support: Nestadt et al. (2010) found 68% concordance for identical twins and 31% for non-identical twins; Lewis (1936) found 37% of OCD patients had a parent with OCD. Limitations: so many genes are involved that it has little predictive value, concordance is not 100%, and environmental risk factors matter (Cromer et al. 2007: over half of OCD patients had a traumatic past event).

Abnormal neurotransmitters: low serotonin and high dopamine. Abnormal brain circuits: the orbitofrontal cortex sends worry signals to the thalamus, which the caudate nucleus normally suppresses; if it is damaged, the worry signals keep firing. The parahippocampal gyrus (unpleasant emotions) is also implicated.

Support: antidepressants that raise serotonin reduce OCD symptoms, and OCD occurs with other disorders that have biological causes (e.g. Parkinson's). Limitations: serotonin is also involved in depression, which is often co-morbid with OCD; and cause and effect are unclear (brain differences may result from OCD).

SSRIs such as fluoxetine (usually 20mg a day) block the reuptake of serotonin into the presynaptic neuron, so more serotonin stays in the synapse and keeps stimulating the postsynaptic neuron. They take 3 to 4 months to work. Alternatives include tricyclics (e.g. clomipramine). Often combined with CBT.

Effective: Soomro et al. (2008) reviewed 17 studies and found SSRIs more effective than placebos. Cheap and not disruptive to daily life. Limitations: side effects (indigestion, blurred vision, loss of sex drive) lead some to stop; it treats symptoms not causes, so relapse can follow when stopping; drug company funding may bias research.

All behaviour is learned from the environment. Only observable behaviour should be studied, using lab experiments. The same basic processes of learning apply to animals and humans, so animals can be studied. We are born a blank slate (tabula rasa).
Learning by association (Pavlov). Food (UCS) produces salivation (UCR). A bell (NS) is repeatedly paired with food. The bell becomes a CS that produces salivation (CR) on its own.

Learning through consequences (Skinner). Positive reinforcement: a reward makes behaviour more likely. Negative reinforcement: escaping or avoiding something unpleasant makes behaviour more likely. Punishment: an unpleasant consequence makes behaviour less likely.
Rats in a Skinner box learned to press a lever when it delivered food (positive reinforcement) or switched off an electric shock (negative reinforcement).

Strengths: scientific credibility (controlled, objective, replicable lab experiments) and real-world applications (token economies, systematic desensitisation). Limitations: environmental determinism ignores free will; it ignores cognition; there are ethical and practical issues with animal research and generalising to humans.
Bandura: we learn directly through conditioning and indirectly by observing and imitating models. Learning involves vicarious reinforcement, identification and mediational (cognitive) processes.
When an observer associates themselves with a role model and wants to be like them, often because the model is similar in age, gender or status.
Learning by observing the consequences of others' behaviour. Behaviour that is rewarded in a model is more likely to be imitated.

Cognitive factors between stimulus and response: attention (noticing the behaviour), retention (remembering it), motor reproduction (being able to perform it) and motivation (wanting to perform it). The first two concern learning, the last two performance.

Children watched an adult behave aggressively (hitting with a mallet, shouting) or non-aggressively towards a Bobo doll. Those who saw the aggressive model were more aggressive later; boys were more aggressive than girls, and same-sex models were imitated more.
Children who saw an aggressive model being rewarded were more aggressive themselves than those who saw the model punished. Supports vicarious reinforcement.

Strengths: it includes cognitive factors, so it is more complete than behaviourism, and it explains cultural differences. Limitations: lab studies such as Bandura's have demand characteristics (a Bobo doll is designed to be hit); it underplays biological factors (e.g. testosterone); Bandura later described reciprocal determinism.

Internal mental processes can and should be studied scientifically. Because they are private, they are studied indirectly by making inferences from behaviour. It uses theoretical and computer models and the concept of schema.

A mental framework of beliefs and expectations built from experience. Schemas let us process information quickly but can distort perception and memory. Babies are born with simple motor schemas such as grasping.

Simplified, often diagrammatic representations of mental processes based on research, such as the multi-store model of memory. Many follow the information processing approach: input, processing, output.
Comparing the mind to a computer, with a central processor, coding and stores. This analogy has been used to develop artificial intelligence.

The scientific study of how brain structures influence mental processes, often using brain scans (e.g. fMRI). Example: Tulving found episodic and semantic memory are linked to different sides of the prefrontal cortex.

Strengths: scientific, objective methods and real-world applications (AI, CBT). Limitations: machine reductionism ignores emotion and motivation; artificial stimuli in lab studies lack external validity; it is soft determinist.
Everything psychological is first biological. Behaviour has a genetic and neurochemical basis. The mind and body are one. Behaviour is a product of evolution.

Genotype: a person's actual genetic make-up. Phenotype: the way genes are expressed in physical, behavioural and psychological characteristics, which is affected by the environment (e.g. PKU can be prevented by diet).
Compare concordance rates for identical (MZ, 100% shared genes) and non-identical (DZ, about 50%) twins. Higher concordance in MZ twins suggests a genetic influence.
Darwin's natural selection: genetically determined behaviours that help survival and reproduction are passed on to future generations, e.g. attachment behaviours.

Strengths: scientific methods (fMRI, EEG, drug trials) and real-world applications (psychoactive drugs). Limitations: causal conclusions are uncertain (a drug working does not prove the chemical caused the disorder); it is biologically determinist and reductionist.
Freud: the unconscious mind drives most behaviour; personality has three parts (id, ego and superego); defence mechanisms protect the ego; childhood psychosexual stages shape adult personality.

The part of the mind we are not aware of, which still drives much of our behaviour. It holds threatening memories that have been repressed and can show itself in dreams and slips of the tongue. The preconscious holds thoughts we can become aware of.
The primitive part of the personality, present at birth. It works on the pleasure principle, is entirely unconscious and demands immediate gratification.
Works on the reality principle and develops at around age 2. It mediates between the id and superego, reducing conflict with defence mechanisms.
Forms at the end of the phallic stage (around age 5). It is our internalised sense of right and wrong, based on the same-sex parent, and works on the morality principle, punishing the ego with guilt.

Unconscious strategies the ego uses to manage conflict between the id and superego. Repression: forcing a distressing memory out of the conscious mind. Denial: refusing to accept reality. Displacement: moving feelings from their real source onto a substitute target.

Oral (0-1, mouth, conflict over weaning), anal (1-3, toilet training), phallic (3-6, genitals, Oedipus or Electra complex), latency (6 to puberty, earlier conflicts repressed), genital (puberty onwards). Unresolved conflict leads to fixation in adulthood (e.g. oral fixation: smoking).

In the phallic stage, boys desire their mother and see their father as a rival, then fear castration. They resolve it by identifying with their father and taking on his gender role and values. Freud's case study of Little Hans.

Strengths: huge explanatory power and influence, and it introduced psychotherapy. Limitations: it is based on case studies (e.g. Little Hans) that are subjective and hard to generalise; its concepts are unfalsifiable (Popper called it pseudoscience); it is psychically determinist.

People have free will and are self-determining. It focuses on the person's subjective experience and the drive to self-actualise, and rejects scientific methods in favour of an idiographic approach. Key figures: Maslow and Rogers.

From bottom to top: physiological needs, safety and security, love and belonging, self-esteem, self-actualisation. Lower deficiency needs must be met before a person can reach self-actualisation, a growth need.
The innate drive to grow psychologically and fulfil one's full potential.
When a person's self-concept (how they see themselves) and ideal self (who they want to be) are similar. A big gap (incongruence) leads to low self-worth and blocks self-actualisation.

Conditions that parents or others put on their love ('I will love you only if...'). They cause incongruence and low self-esteem. Rogers argued people need unconditional positive regard, which client-centred therapy provides along with genuineness and empathy.

Strengths: it is holistic, not reductionist, and has an optimistic view of people. Limitations: limited application beyond counselling, its concepts are hard to test scientifically, and it may be culturally biased because self-actualisation and independence are individualist values.
Comparing approaches: determinism vs free will
Behaviourist (environmental), biological (biological) and psychodynamic (psychic) are hard determinist. SLT and cognitive are soft determinist. Humanistic psychology argues for free will.

Biological: nature. Behaviourist: nurture. SLT: mainly nurture. Cognitive: both (innate schemas refined by experience). Psychodynamic: both (innate drives shaped by childhood experience). Humanistic: mainly nurture (conditions of worth).

Behaviourist (stimulus-response reductionism), biological (biological reductionism), cognitive (machine reductionism) and psychodynamic are reductionist. SLT is less reductionist. Humanistic psychology is holistic.
Humanistic psychology is idiographic; psychodynamic is mainly idiographic (case studies) but proposes general laws. Behaviourist, biological, cognitive and SLT are nomothetic.

Central nervous system (CNS): the brain and spinal cord. Peripheral nervous system (PNS): the somatic nervous system (voluntary movement and senses) and the autonomic nervous system (involuntary functions), which has sympathetic and parasympathetic branches.
Brain: the centre of awareness; the cerebral cortex handles higher mental functions. Spinal cord: passes messages between the brain and PNS and controls simple reflexes.
Carries sensory information from receptors to the CNS and motor commands from the CNS to skeletal muscles. Controls voluntary movement and reflex arcs.

Controls vital involuntary functions such as heart rate, digestion and breathing. The sympathetic branch increases arousal (fight or flight); the parasympathetic branch returns the body to rest ('rest and digest').
Carries messages from sensory receptors to the CNS. Long dendrites and short axons.
Connects sensory neurons to motor neurons or other relay neurons. Found only in the CNS. Short dendrites and short axons.
Connects the CNS to effectors (muscles and glands). Short dendrites and long axons.

Cell body (contains the nucleus), dendrites (receive signals), axon (carries the impulse away from the cell body, covered by a myelin sheath with nodes of Ranvier that speed it up) and terminal buttons (communicate with the next neuron).
At rest the inside of a neuron is negatively charged. When activated, the inside briefly becomes positive, creating an action potential: an electrical impulse that travels down the axon.

The impulse reaches the presynaptic terminal, which releases neurotransmitter from synaptic vesicles. It diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic neuron, where the chemical message becomes electrical again. Leftover neurotransmitter is reabsorbed (reuptake) or broken down by enzymes. Transmission is one-way.
Chemicals that carry signals across the synapse. Each has a specific shape that fits its receptor. Examples: acetylcholine (muscle contraction), serotonin (mood), dopamine (reward and movement).

Excitatory neurotransmitters (e.g. adrenaline, glutamate) make the postsynaptic neuron more positive and more likely to fire. Inhibitory neurotransmitters (e.g. serotonin, GABA) make it more negative and less likely to fire.
Whether a postsynaptic neuron fires depends on the sum of all the excitatory and inhibitory signals it receives. If the net effect is excitatory, it fires.

A network of glands that release hormones directly into the bloodstream to reach target organs. It acts more slowly than the nervous system but its effects last longer. The pituitary is the 'master gland', controlled by the hypothalamus.

Pituitary (ACTH, oxytocin), thyroid (thyroxine, metabolism), adrenal glands (adrenaline for fight or flight, cortisol for stress), pineal (melatonin), ovaries (oestrogen, progesterone), testes (testosterone).

A stressor is detected and the hypothalamus activates the sympathetic nervous system. The adrenal medulla releases adrenaline into the blood, raising heart rate and breathing, dilating pupils, increasing sweating and muscle tension and slowing digestion. The parasympathetic system restores rest once the threat has passed.

A hormone from the adrenal medulla. It raises heart rate (more blood to muscles), raises breathing rate (more oxygen), dilates pupils and releases glucose for energy, preparing the body for immediate action.

Beta bias: Taylor et al. (2000) suggested females 'tend and befriend' (linked to oxytocin). Gray (1988) noted a first 'freeze' response. In modern life the response can be maladaptive, with repeated activation linked to heart disease.

Functional magnetic resonance imaging detects changes in blood oxygen and flow linked to neural activity, producing 3D images of which areas are active. Strengths: no radiation, good spatial resolution (1-2 mm). Limitations: expensive, poor temporal resolution (about 5 seconds), measures blood flow rather than neural activity directly.

Electroencephalogram: electrodes on the scalp record the brain's overall electrical activity as waves. Used to diagnose epilepsy and study sleep. Strengths: excellent temporal resolution (about 1 ms), cheap. Limitation: poor spatial resolution, so it cannot locate the source of activity.

Event-related potentials: brainwave responses to a specific stimulus, isolated from EEG data by averaging out background activity. Strengths: more specific than EEG, excellent temporal resolution. Limitations: lack of standardised methods between studies, and background noise must be removed.

Studying a person's brain after death, often someone with a rare disorder, and comparing it with a typical brain (e.g. Broca's patient 'Tan'). Strengths: detailed study of deep brain areas; generated early theories. Limitations: cause and effect are unclear, and consent can be an issue.
The theory that specific areas of the brain are responsible for specific physical and psychological functions.
The motor cortex in the frontal lobe of both hemispheres. It controls voluntary movement on the opposite side of the body.
The somatosensory cortex in the parietal lobe. It processes sensory information from the skin, such as touch, heat, pressure and pain.
The visual cortex in the occipital lobe. Information from the right visual field goes to the left hemisphere and vice versa.
The auditory cortex in the temporal lobe. It analyses sounds and speech-based information.
In the left frontal lobe, responsible for speech production. Damage causes Broca's aphasia: slow, effortful, non-fluent speech (e.g. Broca's patient 'Tan', 1861).
In the left temporal lobe, responsible for understanding language. Damage causes Wernicke's aphasia: fluent but meaningless speech, often with made-up words, and difficulty understanding.

Support: brain scans (Petersen et al. 1988 found Wernicke's area active when listening and Broca's when reading) and neurosurgery (Dougherty et al. 2002: cingulotomy for OCD). Against: Lashley (1950) removed 10-50% of rats' cortex and found no single area mattered more for maze learning (equipotentiality); language may be more widely distributed (Dick & Tremblay 2016).

The idea that the two hemispheres are functionally different, with some functions mainly in one hemisphere. For example, language is usually in the left hemisphere and visual-spatial processing and face recognition in the right.

Sperry (1968) studied 11 people whose corpus callosum had been cut to treat epilepsy. An image shown to the right visual field (left hemisphere) could be described in words. An image shown to the left visual field (right hemisphere) could not be named but could be drawn or picked out with the left hand.

Strength: highly standardised, controlled procedures. Limitations: small, unusual sample (all had severe epilepsy), confounding variables such as drug history, and lateralisation may change with age (Szaflarski et al. 2006).
The brain's ability to change and adapt through experience and learning. Rarely used connections are deleted (synaptic pruning) and frequently used ones strengthened, throughout life.

Maguire et al. (2000): London taxi drivers had more grey matter in the posterior hippocampus than controls, and this was linked to how long they had driven. Draganski et al. (2006): medical students' brains changed during exam revision.

After damage, healthy areas can take over the functions of damaged areas. Mechanisms: axonal sprouting (new nerve endings connect to undamaged cells), denervation supersensitivity, recruitment of similar (homologous) areas in the opposite hemisphere, and unmasking of dormant synapses.

Real-world application in neurorehabilitation (e.g. constraint-induced movement therapy). Plasticity can be negative (e.g. phantom limb pain, Ramachandran & Hirstein 1998). It declines with age, though Bezzola et al. (2012) found golf training changed motor areas in 40-60 year olds. More education predicts better recovery (Schneider et al. 2014).
An aim is a general statement of what the researcher intends to investigate. A hypothesis is a precise, testable statement of the expected relationship between variables.
States the direction of the difference or relationship (e.g. 'more', 'fewer', 'positive correlation'). Used when previous research suggests what will happen. Analysed with a one-tailed test.
States that there will be a difference or relationship but not which way. Used when there is no previous research or findings conflict. Analysed with a two-tailed test.
States there will be no difference or relationship between the variables. It is what the statistical test assesses.
The variable the researcher manipulates (or that varies naturally) to see its effect on the DV.
The variable the researcher measures. Any change should be caused by the IV.
Any variable other than the IV that might affect the DV if it is not controlled, e.g. noise or time of day.
Defining variables clearly in terms of how they will be measured, e.g. 'memory' becomes 'the number of words correctly recalled from a list of 20'.

Conducted in a controlled environment; the researcher manipulates the IV and records the DV. Strengths: high control, so cause and effect can be shown, and easy to replicate. Limitations: may lack ecological validity; demand characteristics.

The IV is manipulated by the researcher in a natural, everyday setting. Strengths: higher mundane realism and more natural behaviour. Limitations: less control of extraneous variables; ethical issues (no consent, invasion of privacy).

The researcher takes advantage of an IV that varies naturally, not manipulated by them (e.g. children in orphanages). Strengths: allows research that would be unethical otherwise and often has high external validity. Limitations: the event may be rare, so hard to replicate; no random allocation.

The IV is a difference that already exists between people (e.g. age, gender, having a disorder). Strength: often carried out under controlled conditions. Limitation: no random allocation, so confounding variables are possible and causation is uncertain.

The same participants take part in all conditions. Strengths: participant variables are controlled and fewer participants are needed. Limitations: order effects (practice, boredom, fatigue) and participants may guess the aim. Order effects are controlled by counterbalancing.

Different participants take part in each condition. Strengths: no order effects and less chance of guessing the aim. Limitations: participant variables may differ between groups, and more participants are needed. Controlled by random allocation.

Participants are paired on key variables (e.g. IQ) and one of each pair goes into each condition. Strengths: reduces participant variables and has no order effects. Limitation: matching is time-consuming and never perfect.
A way to control order effects in repeated measures. Half the participants do condition A then B and the other half do B then A (or every participant does A, B, B, A).
Each participant has an equal chance of being placed in each condition, which controls participant variables in an independent groups design.
Using exactly the same procedures and instructions for all participants, so differences in the DV are not caused by differences in procedure.
Using chance to decide things such as the order of conditions or materials, to reduce researcher bias.
A group that does not receive the IV or treatment, used as a baseline for comparison.
Cues that reveal the aim of a study to participants, who may then change their behaviour to please the researcher or to spoil the results. Reduced by a single-blind procedure.
Any effect of the investigator's behaviour on the outcome (the DV), such as leading questions, body language or how participants are chosen. Reduced by a double-blind procedure.
Single-blind: participants do not know the aim or which condition they are in. Double-blind: neither the participants nor the person running the study know, which also reduces investigator effects.
The target population is the group the researcher wants to study and generalise to. A sample is a smaller group drawn from it to take part, which should be representative.

Every member of the target population has an equal chance of being selected (e.g. a random number generator). Strength: free from researcher bias. Limitations: hard and time-consuming, needs a full list of the population, and people may refuse.
Every nth person on a list of the target population is selected. Strength: avoids researcher bias. Limitation: may still be unrepresentative by chance.

The sample reflects the proportions of sub-groups (strata) in the population, e.g. if 40% are under 30, 40% of the sample are; people are then picked randomly within each stratum. Strength: representative. Limitations: cannot reflect every way people differ; time-consuming.
Selecting whoever is available and willing at the time. Strengths: quick, easy and cheap. Limitations: unrepresentative, and researcher bias in who is approached.

Participants select themselves, e.g. by replying to an advert. Strength: easy, and participants are engaged. Limitation: volunteer bias, since volunteers may share traits such as being curious or keen to help.
Bias happens when some groups are over- or under-represented in a sample. This limits generalisation: how far findings can be applied to the target population.
A small trial run before the main study to check procedures, materials and instructions work, so changes can be made before time and money are spent.
Behaviour is observed in the setting where it normally occurs, without interference. Strength: high external validity. Limitation: little control, so hard to replicate.
Behaviour is observed in a structured setting where some variables are controlled (e.g. the Strange Situation). Strength: easier to replicate. Limitation: the setting may be artificial.
Covert: participants do not know they are being watched, so behaviour is natural, but this raises ethical issues. Overt: participants know, which is more ethical, but they may change their behaviour.

Participant: the researcher joins the group being studied, gaining insight but risking 'going native' and losing objectivity. Non-participant: the researcher stays separate, which is more objective but gives less insight.
Breaking a target behaviour into observable, measurable components, e.g. 'affection' becomes hugging, kissing and smiling. They should be clear, not overlap and cover all possible behaviours.
Recording every time a target behaviour occurs. Strength: good for behaviours that happen rarely. Limitation: complex behaviours may be missed if too much happens at once.

Recording behaviour at set intervals, e.g. every 30 seconds. Strength: reduces the number of observations. Limitation: behaviour outside the intervals is missed, so the record may be unrepresentative.

The extent to which two or more observers agree. They observe the same behaviour separately using the same categories and their tallies are correlated; a correlation of +0.8 or more shows good reliability.

A set of written questions used to assess thoughts and experiences. Strengths: can collect a lot of data quickly and cheaply, without the researcher present. Limitations: social desirability bias and response bias (e.g. acquiescence bias).

Open questions have no fixed answers and produce qualitative data, which is rich but hard to analyse. Closed questions have fixed answers (e.g. Likert scales, rating scales) and produce quantitative data, which is easy to analyse but may lack depth.
A closed question where respondents rate their agreement with a statement, usually on a 5-point scale from strongly agree to strongly disagree.
Pre-set questions asked in a fixed order. Strength: easy to replicate and less interviewer bias. Limitation: the interviewer cannot follow up interesting answers.
No fixed questions, just a topic, like a conversation; the interviewer can probe further. Strength: rich detail. Limitations: more interviewer bias, harder to analyse.
Use an interview schedule (a standard list of questions), a quiet setting, build rapport with neutral opening questions, and keep answers confidential.
Avoid jargon, emotive or leading questions, double-barrelled questions (two questions in one) and double negatives. Use filler questions to hide the aim and start with easy questions.
A technique that shows the strength and direction of an association between two co-variables. There is no IV or DV. Shown on a scattergram as positive, negative or zero.

In an experiment the researcher manipulates an IV and measures its effect on a DV, so cause and effect can be shown. In a correlation, two co-variables are measured without manipulation, so causation cannot be shown because a third variable might explain the link.
Strengths: quick and economical, can use existing data, and identifies relationships to test further. Limitations: no cause and effect, and intervening variables may explain the relationship.

A number from -1 to +1 showing the direction and strength of a correlation. +1 is a perfect positive correlation, -1 is a perfect negative correlation and 0 is no correlation. +0.2 is weak positive; -0.8 is strong negative.

An indirect way of studying behaviour by analysing communications people produce, such as texts, TV or books. Coding puts material into categories and counts them (quantitative). Thematic analysis identifies recurring themes (qualitative).

Strengths: high external validity because it uses real communications, and few ethical issues because the material already exists. Limitations: material is studied out of context, so the researcher may misinterpret it, and thematic analysis can be subjective.

An in-depth study of one person, group, institution or event, often over a long period (e.g. HM). Mainly qualitative data from interviews and observations. Strengths: rich detail, and allow study of rare cases. Limitations: hard to generalise, subjective interpretation and reliance on memory.

Qualitative data are words (e.g. interview transcripts): rich and detailed but hard to analyse objectively. Quantitative data are numbers (e.g. reaction times): easy to analyse and more objective but may miss meaning.

Primary data are collected by the researcher for this study, so they fit the aims but take effort. Secondary data were collected by someone else (e.g. government statistics), so they are cheap and quick but may be inaccurate or not fit the aims.

Combining the results of many studies on a topic to reach an overall statistical conclusion (an effect size). Strength: a larger sample makes conclusions more generalisable. Limitation: publication bias (the file drawer problem), as non-significant studies often go unpublished.
Add all the scores and divide by the number of scores. Strength: uses all the data, so it is the most sensitive. Limitation: distorted by extreme values. Suits interval data.
The middle value when scores are put in order (average the two middle values if there is an even number). Strength: not affected by extreme scores. Limitation: less sensitive. Suits ordinal data.
The most frequent value. Strength: easy, and the only measure for nominal data. Limitation: crude, and there may be more than one mode.
The highest value minus the lowest value. Strength: easy to calculate. Limitation: affected by extreme values and says nothing about how data are spread around the mean.

The average spread of scores around the mean. A large SD means scores are widely spread; a small SD means they are close to the mean. Strength: more precise than the range as it uses all scores. Limitation: can be distorted by extreme values.
Percentage = (part ÷ whole) × 100. Percentage change = ((new − old) ÷ old) × 100.
Bar charts show discrete categories (e.g. nominal data) with gaps between bars. Histograms show continuous data, with bars touching, equal-width intervals on the x-axis and no gaps.
Used for correlations. Each point represents a pair of values for the two co-variables.
A symmetrical bell-shaped curve where the mean, median and mode are all at the centre. Most scores are near the middle and the tails never touch the x-axis.
Most scores are bunched at the low end, with a long tail to the right (e.g. a very hard test). Mode < median < mean, as the mean is pulled towards the tail.
Most scores are bunched at the high end, with a long tail to the left (e.g. a very easy test). Mean < median < mode.
Data in separate categories, such as favourite colour; each item fits only one category. Use the mode.
Data that can be ranked but where intervals are not equal, such as ratings on a scale of 1 to 10. Use the median.
Data measured on a scale with equal, precisely defined units, such as time or temperature. Use the mean and standard deviation.
Testing for a difference, with a related design (repeated measures or matched pairs) and nominal data (or data turned into + and − signs).

1) Work out the difference between each pair of scores and record its sign (+ or −). 2) Discard any zero differences and reduce N. 3) S is the number of the less frequent sign. 4) The result is significant if S is equal to or less than the critical value.
Psychologists usually use p ≤ 0.05: there is a 5% or lower probability that the result is due to chance. A stricter p ≤ 0.01 is used when being wrong would be costly, such as in drug trials.
The value a test statistic must reach for the null hypothesis to be rejected. Found in a table using: one- or two-tailed test, N (or degrees of freedom) and the significance level.
A false positive: rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true, claiming an effect that is really due to chance. More likely with a lenient significance level (e.g. 10%).
A false negative: accepting the null hypothesis when it is false, missing a real effect. More likely with a strict significance level (e.g. 1%).

Ask three questions: 1) Is it a test of difference or correlation? 2) If difference, is the design related (repeated measures or matched pairs) or unrelated (independent groups)? 3) What is the level of measurement: nominal, ordinal or interval?
Unrelated difference: Chi-Squared. Related difference: Sign test. Association: Chi-Squared.
Unrelated difference: Mann-Whitney. Related difference: Wilcoxon. Correlation: Spearman's rho.
Unrelated difference: unrelated t-test. Related difference: related t-test. Correlation: Pearson's r. These are parametric tests, which also need normally distributed data and similar variances.

If the test name contains an R (Spearman's, Pearson's, Chi-Squared, unrelated and related t-tests), the calculated value must be greater than or equal to the critical value. For Sign test, Wilcoxon and Mann-Whitney it must be equal to or less than the critical value.
The British Psychological Society's code is built on four principles: respect, competence, responsibility and integrity. Ethics committees weigh costs against benefits before approving research.

Participants should know the aims, procedures, their rights (including the right to withdraw) and how their data will be used before agreeing. Alternatives where full consent would spoil the study: presumptive, prior general or retrospective consent. Parental consent is needed for under-16s.

Deliberately misleading participants or withholding information. Acceptable only if it causes no undue distress. Dealt with by a full debrief, revealing the true aim and offering the right to withdraw data.
Participants should face no more risk than in everyday life, physically or psychologically. Dealt with by reminding them of their right to withdraw, debriefing, and offering counselling if needed.

Participants have the right to control information about themselves, and personal data must be protected (Data Protection Act / GDPR). Dealt with by anonymity (using numbers or initials) and not recording identifying details.

Experts in the same field anonymously assess a piece of research before it is published, to check its quality. It is used to allocate research funding, validate the quality and relevance of research, and suggest improvements.

Limitations: anonymity can let reviewers criticise rivals unfairly; publication bias favours positive, headline-grabbing findings; groundbreaking work may be rejected because it challenges established ideas; flawed findings remain once published.
Implications of research for the economy

Research can benefit the economy. Attachment research shows fathers can be primary caregivers, so both parents can work flexibly. Research into mental health treatments (e.g. CBT, drugs) helps people return to work sooner, reducing the cost of absence.
How consistent a measure or test is: whether it produces the same results each time it is used.
Giving the same test to the same people on two occasions, with enough time between (e.g. two weeks). The scores are correlated and +0.8 or above shows good reliability.

Questionnaires: rewrite ambiguous questions, use more closed questions. Interviews: use the same trained interviewer and structured interviews. Experiments: standardised procedures. Observations: clearly operationalised, non-overlapping categories and trained observers.
Whether a finding is genuine: whether a measure tests what it claims to (internal validity) and whether findings generalise beyond the study (external validity).
Whether a test appears, at face value, to measure what it claims to. Checked by looking at it or asking an expert.

Whether a new measure gives similar results to an existing, well-established measure of the same thing. Participants take both and the scores are correlated; +0.8 or above suggests good concurrent validity.
How far findings can be generalised from the research setting to other settings, especially everyday life.
How far findings from a study stay true over time, e.g. whether Asch's 1950s findings apply today.

Experiments: use a control group, standardised procedures and single- or double-blind designs. Questionnaires: anonymity and lie scales to reduce social desirability. Observations: covert observation and clear categories. Qualitative research: triangulation and direct quotes.

Objectivity: researchers keep a critical distance so their personal views do not bias the data. The empirical method: knowledge is gained through direct observation and measurement, not argument or belief.
The extent to which other researchers can repeat a study's procedures and get the same results. It requires detailed reporting of methods.
Popper: a theory is only scientific if it could, in principle, be proved false. Scientific theories put themselves up for testing. Freud's theory is often criticised as unfalsifiable.
A theory is a set of general principles that explain behaviour. It is built from evidence gathered through observation, and generates hypotheses that can be tested; the theory is then refined.

Kuhn (1962): a paradigm is a set of shared assumptions and methods within a science. A paradigm shift is a scientific revolution where the dominant theory is replaced because contradictory evidence builds up. Kuhn argued psychology lacks a single paradigm (it is a 'pre-science').
A short summary (150-200 words) at the start covering the aims, hypotheses, method, results and conclusions.
A review of relevant theories and research, moving from broad to specific and leading logically to the aims and hypotheses.

Enough detail for replication: design (with justification), sample (participants, sampling method, target population), materials, procedure (including standardised instructions, briefing and debriefing) and ethics.

Descriptive statistics (tables, graphs, central tendency and dispersion) and inferential statistics (the test used, calculated and critical values, significance level and whether the null hypothesis is accepted or rejected). Raw data go in an appendix.
Summarises the results in words, relates them to previous research, considers limitations and improvements, and discusses wider real-world implications.
Full details of all sources cited. For a journal article: author(s), date, title, journal (in italics), volume and page numbers.
The aim to develop theories that apply to all people, regardless of gender or culture. Gender and cultural bias threaten universality.
Representing or treating men and women differently in ways based on stereotypes rather than real differences.
Male-centred research: 'normal' behaviour is judged by a male standard, so female behaviour is seen as abnormal or inferior.
Exaggerating differences between men and women, often devaluing women. Example: Freud's claim that women have a weaker superego.

Ignoring or minimising differences between men and women, often by studying only men and assuming the findings apply to women. Example: early fight or flight research (Taylor et al. 2000 proposed 'tend and befriend' in females).

Biased research can be used to justify discrimination (e.g. against women at work). Researchers have been mostly male. Feminist psychology aims to correct bias by studying women in real-life contexts and treating participants as collaborators (Worell 1992). Reflexivity means researchers acknowledge their own values.
Ignoring cultural differences and interpreting all behaviour through the lens of one's own culture, usually Western.
Judging other cultures by the standards of one's own, assuming it is superior. Example: the Strange Situation treats American-style secure attachment as ideal.
The idea that norms, values and behaviour can only be properly understood within their own social and cultural context.

Etic: studying behaviour from outside a culture to find universal behaviours. Emic: studying from inside a culture to identify behaviours specific to it. Imposed etic: using a method developed in one culture to study another (e.g. the Strange Situation in Japan).

The individualist-collectivist distinction may be outdated (Takano & Osaka 1999 found 14 of 15 studies showed no difference between the US and Japan). Some behaviours may be universal (e.g. facial expressions of emotion). Participants from other cultures may be unfamiliar with research, creating demand characteristics.
The idea that humans can make their own choices and are not entirely controlled by biological or environmental forces (the humanistic view).
All behaviour is caused by internal or external forces beyond our control, so free will is impossible.
All behaviour has a cause, but people still have some conscious choice within certain limits (William James). The cognitive approach takes this view.
Behaviour is caused by biological factors we cannot control, such as genes, hormones and neurotransmitters.
Behaviour is caused by features of the environment, such as reinforcement and punishment. Skinner said free will is an illusion.
Behaviour is caused by unconscious conflicts we cannot control (Freud).
Science assumes every event has a cause and aims to discover general laws. Determinism fits the aims of science, as lab experiments manipulate an IV to find its effect.

Free will has face validity, and an internal locus of control is linked to better mental health (Roberts et al. 1987). But Libet et al. (1983) found brain activity for a decision occurred before conscious awareness. Hard determinism fits science but not the legal system, which holds people responsible, and it is unfalsifiable.
The debate over how far behaviour is caused by inherited characteristics (nature) or by environment and experience (nurture).
A number from 0 to 1 showing how far a characteristic is due to genes; 1.0 means entirely genetic. IQ is about 0.5.

Nature and nurture interact. Examples: the diathesis-stress model (genetic vulnerability plus an environmental trigger); epigenetics (the environment changes how genes are expressed, which can be passed on); niche picking (people seek environments that suit their genetic tendencies).
Lerner (1986): the environment ranges from prenatal factors (e.g. a mother smoking) to postnatal experiences such as social conditions and culture.

Extreme nativist views have been linked to eugenics; empiricist views suggest any behaviour can be changed. Shared and non-shared environments make the two hard to separate. Plomin's idea of constructivism: people create their own nurture by their choices.
The view that a system should be studied as a whole rather than as separate parts, because the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. Example: humanistic psychology.
The view that behaviour is best explained by breaking it down into its simplest parts (the principle of parsimony).

Behaviour can be explained at different levels, from the highest (social and cultural) to the lowest (biological and neurochemical). Example for OCD: cultural, psychological (thoughts), physical (compulsions), physiological (brain circuits), neurochemical (serotonin).
Explaining behaviour in terms of neurons, neurotransmitters, hormones, brain structure or genes. Example: explaining OCD by low serotonin.
Explaining behaviour as simple learned links between stimulus and response, ignoring mental processes (behaviourism).

Holism: some behaviour only appears in groups (e.g. crowd behaviour), but holistic accounts are hard to test. Reductionism: scientific, allows variables to be operationalised and led to drug treatments, but it can oversimplify and ignore the meaning or context of behaviour.
Studying individuals in depth as unique cases, usually with qualitative methods such as case studies and unstructured interviews. Used by humanistic psychology and Freud.
Studying large groups to establish general laws of behaviour, using quantitative methods and statistics. Used by behaviourist, biological and cognitive psychologists.

Idiographic research is detailed and can generate hypotheses, but it is hard to generalise and less scientific. Nomothetic research is scientific and replicable but loses the individual person. The two can complement each other.
Sieber and Stanley (1988): research with potential social consequences for participants or for the group of people they represent, such as research into race, sexuality or intelligence.

Sieber and Stanley: implications (wider effects, e.g. justifying discrimination), uses (how findings may be used in public policy), validity (are findings sound? e.g. Burt's fraudulent IQ data) and how research questions are framed.

Socially sensitive research can benefit groups that are under-represented and challenge stereotypes, so it should not be avoided (Scarr 1988). But poor research has justified discrimination (e.g. Yerkes' army IQ tests influencing US immigration laws). Ethics committees weigh costs and benefits, but these are hard to predict.

Revealing personal information to a partner. Social penetration theory (Altman & Taylor 1973): disclosure gradually increases in breadth then depth, like peeling an onion, and reciprocal disclosure builds intimacy.

Support: Sprecher and Hendrick (2004) found strong correlations between self-disclosure and satisfaction in dating couples. Limitations: the research is correlational, and there are cultural differences (Tang et al. 2013: Americans disclose more sexual thoughts than people in China, yet satisfaction is similar).

Important in initial attraction. Symmetrical faces are seen as attractive (a sign of genetic fitness) and baby-faced (neotenous) features trigger protectiveness. The halo effect: attractive people are assumed to have other good traits (Dion et al. 1972).

Walster et al. (1966): people choose partners of similar physical attractiveness to themselves, balancing the wish for an attractive partner against the fear of rejection, based on a realistic view of their own 'value'.
