Macroeconomic policies in a global context

Policies to reduce fiscal deficits and national debt, reduce poverty and inequality, change interest rates and the money supply, control global companies' pricing (transfer pricing), and respond to external shocks.
Inaccurate information, risks and uncertainty, and the inability to control external shocks (e.g. global recessions, oil price changes).

exam.q: Explain what is meant by internalisation and compliance. Use an example of each.
points: Internalisation: genuine acceptance of group norms
Internalisation: private and public change, lasting without the group
Compliance: going along publicly while privately disagreeing
Compliance: temporary, stops when the group pressure is gone
Relevant example for each (e.g. adopting vegetarian beliefs vs laughing at a joke you don't find funny)
exam.tip: 2 marks each: 1 for a clear definition, 1 for a fitting example or elaboration.

exam.q: Discuss situational variables affecting obedience. Refer to research in your answer.
points: Proximity: teacher and learner in same room 40%, touch proximity 30%, remote instructions 20.5%
Location: run-down office block in Bridgeport 47.5% vs 65% at Yale
Uniform: experimenter replaced by member of the public in ordinary clothes, 20%
Explanation of why each variable matters (e.g. buffer, legitimacy of authority)
AO3: support from Bickman (1974) field experiment on uniform
AO3: cross-cultural support (e.g. Miranda et al. 1981, over 90% in Spain)
AO3: Orne and Holland, participants may have realised the procedure was fake (especially uniform variation)
AO3: situational explanation ignores dispositional factors (Mandel's 'obedience alibi', Authoritarian Personality)
AO3: high control of variables in the variations allows cause and effect
levels: Knowledge accurate and generally well detailed. Discussion thorough and effective. Clear, coherent and focused. Specialist terminology used effectively.
Knowledge evident with occasional inaccuracy. Discussion mostly effective. Mostly clear and organised. Terminology mostly used appropriately.
Limited knowledge, some relevant. Discussion apparent but mostly ineffective. Lacks clarity and organisation in places.
Very limited knowledge. Discussion limited, poorly focused or absent.
exam.tip: Pick 2-3 variables and describe them with figures (AO1), then spend most of your time on 4-5 developed evaluation points: point, evidence, explain why it matters.

exam.q: Sam is learning French vocabulary for a test, but when he tries to recall the words he keeps remembering the Spanish words he learned last year instead. Outline proactive interference and explain how it applies to Sam's experience.
points: Proactive interference: old learning disrupts new learning
Most likely when the two sets of material are similar
Interference is an explanation of forgetting in LTM
Application: Sam's Spanish (old) blocks the French (new)
Application: the languages are similar, so interference is greater
Application: e.g. he could space learning or use distinct cues
exam.tip: For application questions, keep linking back to the stem ('Sam...'). A general answer with no link caps you at about half marks.

exam.q: Describe and evaluate the working memory model.
points: Central executive: supervises, allocates attention, very limited capacity
Phonological loop: phonological store and articulatory process; about 2 seconds
Visuo-spatial sketchpad: visual cache and inner scribe (Logie)
Episodic buffer: added 2000, integrates information, links to LTM
AO3: clinical evidence, KF had poor verbal STM but intact visual STM
AO3: dual-task research (Baddeley et al. 1975) supports separate slave systems
AO3: word length effect supports the phonological loop
AO3: central executive is vague and poorly defined
AO3: brain-damaged case studies may not generalise; artificial lab tasks
levels: Knowledge accurate and generally well detailed. Discussion thorough and effective. Clear, coherent and focused. Specialist terminology used effectively.
Knowledge evident with occasional inaccuracy. Discussion mostly effective. Mostly clear and organised.
Limited knowledge, some relevant. Discussion apparent but mostly ineffective.
Very limited knowledge. Discussion limited, poorly focused or absent.
exam.tip: A labelled description of all four components gets you the AO1. For AO3, explain what each piece of evidence shows about the model, not just what the study found.

exam.q: Discuss research into the effects of institutionalisation.
points: Rutter's ERA study: 165 Romanian orphans; adopted after 6 months showed disinhibited attachment and lower IQ
Adopted before 6 months: no lasting differences
Zeanah et al. (2005) Bucharest Early Intervention Project: 19% secure vs 74% controls
Effects: disinhibited attachment, intellectual disability, poor peer relationships
AO3: real-world application, improved care in institutions, early adoption, key workers
AO3: Romanian orphanages were unusually extreme, so results may not generalise
AO3: fewer confounding variables than earlier studies (children not usually traumatised before institution)
AO3: lack of adult data in early studies; long-term effects unclear
AO3: natural experiment, no random allocation (adoptive families may differ)
levels: Knowledge accurate and well detailed. Discussion thorough and effective. Clear and coherent.
Knowledge evident with occasional inaccuracy. Discussion mostly effective.
Limited knowledge, some relevant. Discussion mostly ineffective.
Very limited knowledge. Discussion limited or absent.
exam.tip: Use precise findings (6 months, IQ 77 vs 102). Then evaluate the research methods as well as the conclusions.

exam.q: Outline the cognitive characteristics of depression.
points: Poor concentration (e.g. hard to stick to tasks or make decisions)
Attending to and dwelling on the negative (negative bias)
Recalling unhappy events more than happy ones
Absolutist, black-and-white thinking
exam.tip: Only cognitive characteristics count. Lethargy (behavioural) or low mood (emotional) would get no credit.

exam.q: Describe and evaluate the biological approach to explaining and treating OCD.
points: Genetic: polygenic, candidate genes SERT and COMT, aetiologically heterogeneous
Neural: low serotonin, high dopamine; worry circuit (orbitofrontal cortex, caudate nucleus, thalamus)
Drug therapy: SSRIs block reuptake of serotonin, increasing levels in the synapse; 3-4 months
AO3: twin evidence, Nestadt et al. (2010) 68% MZ vs 31% DZ concordance
AO3: concordance not 100%, so environment matters (Cromer et al. 2007)
AO3: neural, causation unclear; co-morbidity with depression
AO3: Soomro et al. (2008), SSRIs more effective than placebo
AO3: side effects; treats symptoms not causes; relapse
AO3: cost-effective, non-disruptive compared with psychological therapy
levels: Knowledge accurate and well detailed. Discussion thorough and effective.
Knowledge evident with occasional inaccuracy. Discussion mostly effective.
Limited knowledge. Discussion mostly ineffective.
Very limited knowledge. Discussion limited or absent.
exam.tip: New 2027 spec wording: 'the biological approach to explaining and treating OCD'. Cover both explanations and the treatment, and balance your evaluation across them.

exam.q: Maya has an extreme fear of dogs. She crosses the road whenever she sees one, and this started after she was bitten as a child. Explain how the two-process model accounts for Maya's phobia.
points: Acquisition by classical conditioning: neutral stimulus paired with an unconditioned stimulus causing fear
Application: dog (NS) paired with bite and pain (UCS) producing fear (UCR); dog becomes CS producing fear (CR)
Maintenance by operant conditioning: negative reinforcement
Application: crossing the road (avoidance) removes her anxiety, which reinforces the avoidance
Generalisation: may fear all dogs, not just the one that bit her
Avoidance prevents extinction because she never learns dogs are safe
levels: Knowledge accurate with some detail. Application clear and effective. Terminology used effectively.
Knowledge evident. Application mostly clear.
Limited knowledge. Application limited.
Very limited knowledge. Application absent or inappropriate.
exam.tip: Label UCS, UCR, NS, CS and CR with Maya's specific details.

exam.q: Compare the behaviourist approach and humanistic psychology.
points: Behaviourism: all behaviour is learned through conditioning; only observable behaviour studied
Humanistic: free will, self-actualisation, subjective experience (Maslow, Rogers)
Determinism vs free will: behaviourism is hard (environmental) determinist; humanistic assumes free will
Methods: behaviourism uses lab experiments (nomothetic); humanistic is idiographic
Reductionism: S-R reductionism vs holism
Nature-nurture: both emphasise environment/nurture (conditions of worth vs reinforcement)
Applications: token economies and SD vs client-centred therapy
Scientific credibility: behaviourism more scientific; humanistic concepts untestable
Cultural bias: humanistic values are individualist
levels: Knowledge accurate and well detailed. Comparison thorough and effective. Clear and coherent.
Knowledge evident. Comparison mostly effective.
Limited knowledge. Comparison mostly ineffective.
Very limited knowledge. Comparison limited or absent.
exam.tip: A 'compare' question rewards point-by-point comparison (similarities and differences) using debates such as free will, reductionism and methodology. Avoid writing two separate essays.

exam.q: Explain the process of synaptic transmission.
points: Impulse arrives at the presynaptic terminal
Vesicles release neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft
Neurotransmitter diffuses across and binds to receptor sites on the postsynaptic neuron
Chemical message converted back to an electrical impulse; excitatory or inhibitory effect
Reuptake or breakdown by enzymes
exam.tip: Use a clear sequence with correct terms: presynaptic, vesicles, synaptic cleft, receptors, postsynaptic.

exam.q: Evaluate split-brain research into hemispheric lateralisation.
points: Strength: standardised, highly controlled procedures (e.g. image flashed for one-tenth of a second to one visual field)
Strength: contributed to understanding that the left hemisphere is mainly for language, right for visual-spatial tasks
Limitation: small sample of 11 with epilepsy, so unusual brains; generalisation is limited
Limitation: confounding variables such as drug history and extent of surgery differed
Limitation: lateralisation may change with age and plasticity
levels: Evaluation thorough and effective. Clear and coherent.
Evaluation mostly effective.
Evaluation limited.
Evaluation very limited.
exam.tip: AO3 only: no marks for describing Sperry's procedure unless it is used to make an evaluative point.

exam.q: A psychologist used a repeated measures design to test whether music affects concentration. 12 participants did a puzzle in silence and with music. 8 did better in silence, 3 did better with music and 1 scored the same. Calculate the value of S for a sign test and state whether the result is significant if the critical value is 1 (N = 11, two-tailed, p ≤ 0.05).
points: Remove the tied score, so N = 11
Signs: 8 one way, 3 the other
S = 3 (the less frequent sign)
3 is greater than the critical value of 1, so the result is not significant; accept the null hypothesis
exam.tip: For the sign test, S must be EQUAL TO OR LESS THAN the critical value to be significant.

exam.q: Explain what is meant by a Type I and a Type II error, and why psychologists usually use the 5% level of significance.
points: Type I error: rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true (false positive)
More likely with a lenient significance level such as 10%
Type II error: accepting the null hypothesis when it is false (false negative)
More likely with a strict significance level such as 1%
5% balances the risk of making a Type I or Type II error
A stricter level (1%) is used when the consequences of error are serious (e.g. drug trials)
exam.tip: Link each error to the significance level that makes it more likely.

exam.q: Discuss the nature-nurture debate in psychology. Refer to at least two topics you have studied.
points: Nature: behaviour determined by heredity; heritability coefficient
Nurture: environmental influences (Lerner's levels of environment)
Interactionist approach: diathesis-stress, epigenetics, niche picking
Examples: schizophrenia genetics (Gottesman) vs family dysfunction
Examples: attachment, Bowlby (innate) vs learning theory
AO3: implications, nativist views linked to eugenics; empiricist views imply behaviour can be changed
AO3: shared and non-shared environments make it hard to separate the two
AO3: constructivism, people create their own environments
AO3: interactionist position is more realistic, e.g. Tienari et al. (2004)
levels: Knowledge accurate and well detailed. Discussion thorough and effective.
Knowledge evident. Discussion mostly effective.
Limited knowledge. Discussion mostly ineffective.
Very limited knowledge. Discussion limited or absent.
exam.tip: Issues and debates questions reward examples from across the course. Use 2-3 topics and keep linking them back to the debate.

exam.q: Describe and evaluate Rusbult's investment model of commitment, satisfaction, comparison with alternatives and investment.
points: Commitment depends on satisfaction, comparison with alternatives and investment size
Satisfaction based on comparison level: rewards outweigh costs
Investment: intrinsic (time, money, disclosure) and extrinsic (children, shared friends)
Commitment leads to maintenance mechanisms (accommodation, derogating alternatives, positive illusions)
AO3: Le and Agnew (2003) meta-analysis of 52 studies, all three factors predict commitment
AO3: explains abusive relationships (Rusbult and Martz 1995)
AO3: Goodfriend and Agnew (2008), future plans also count as investment
AO3: relies on self-report and correlational data
AO3: more comprehensive than social exchange theory
levels: Knowledge accurate and well detailed. Discussion thorough and effective.
Knowledge evident. Discussion mostly effective.
Limited knowledge. Discussion mostly ineffective.
Very limited knowledge. Discussion limited or absent.
exam.tip: Name all three factors explicitly and explain how they combine to produce commitment.

exam.q: Discuss the interactionist approach to explaining and treating schizophrenia.
points: Biological, psychological and social factors all contribute
Diathesis-stress model: vulnerability plus trigger
Original Meehl (1962) single schizogene; modern: polygenic, early trauma as diathesis
Stressors: cannabis, expressed emotion, urban living
Treatment combines antipsychotics with CBT or family therapy
AO3: Tienari et al. (2004) adoption study supports gene-environment interaction
AO3: Tarrier et al. (2004) drugs plus CBT more effective than drugs alone
AO3: original diathesis-stress model oversimplified
AO3: exact mechanism of interaction unclear; treatment-causation fallacy
levels: Knowledge accurate and well detailed. Discussion thorough and effective.
Knowledge evident. Discussion mostly effective.
Limited knowledge. Discussion mostly ineffective.
Very limited knowledge. Discussion limited or absent.
exam.tip: Cover explaining AND treating, as the question asks for both.

exam.q: Describe and evaluate Eysenck's theory of the criminal personality.
points: Three dimensions: extraversion, neuroticism, psychoticism
Criminal personality: neurotic-extravert, high psychoticism
Biological basis: extraverts underaroused nervous system, seek stimulation; neurotics reactive SNS
Socialisation: poor conditioning, so fail to learn to delay gratification
Measured with the EPQ
AO3: Eysenck and Eysenck (1977) prisoners scored higher on E, N and P
AO3: Farrington et al. (1982) only P was consistently higher
AO3: cultural bias, Bartol and Holanchock (1979)
AO3: personality may not be consistent; reductionist; self-report measure
levels: Knowledge accurate and well detailed. Discussion thorough and effective.
Knowledge evident. Discussion mostly effective.
Limited knowledge. Discussion mostly ineffective.
Very limited knowledge. Discussion limited or absent.
exam.tip: Explain the biological basis and the role of socialisation; that is what separates a top-band description.

exam.q: Outline and evaluate restorative justice programmes as a way of dealing with offending behaviour.
points: Offender meets victim (directly or indirectly) with a trained mediator
Offender takes responsibility and sees the impact; victim has a voice
Can include restitution; voluntary
AO3: Restorative Justice Council 85% victim satisfaction
AO3: reoffending reduced by about 14% (Ministry of Justice 2011)
AO3: offenders may take part insincerely; victims may be distressed; unsuitable for some crimes
levels: Knowledge accurate with some detail. Evaluation thorough and effective.
Knowledge evident. Evaluation mostly effective.
Limited knowledge. Evaluation limited.
Very limited knowledge or evaluation.
exam.tip: With 5 marks for AO3, aim for two well-developed evaluation points rather than four brief ones.

exam.q: The price of a train ticket rises from £40 to £50, and the number of tickets sold falls from 2,000 to 1,800 per day. Calculate the price elasticity of demand and explain what it means for the train company's revenue.
points: % change in quantity = −10%
% change in price = +25%
Demand is price inelastic (|PED| < 1)
Total revenue rises: from £80,000 to £90,000
exam.tip: Show your working: formula, both percentage changes and the answer. Then interpret it in context.

exam.q: With the help of a diagram, explain why the free market leads to over-consumption of a good with negative externalities, such as sugary drinks.
points: Negative externality: cost to third parties not reflected in price (e.g. NHS costs of obesity)
Diagram: MSC above MPC (or MPB above MSB for consumption externality)
Market equilibrium at Q1 where MPC = MPB
Social optimum at Q* where MSC = MSB
Q1 > Q*: over-consumption
Welfare loss triangle shown correctly
Consumers ignore external costs, and information gaps may add to over-consumption
exam.tip: Label axes (Price/Costs/Benefits and Quantity), both curves, both quantities and shade the welfare loss.

exam.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of a tax on sugary drinks as a way of reducing obesity.
points: Explain the tax internalises the externality: supply shifts left, price rises, quantity falls towards social optimum
Diagram of indirect tax with incidence on consumers and producers
Revenue can fund NHS or school sports (hypothecation)
UK Soft Drinks Industry Levy encouraged reformulation (firms cut sugar)
Evaluation: PED for sugary drinks may be inelastic, so small fall in consumption
Evaluation: regressive, hits low-income households hardest
Evaluation: hard to set the tax at the right level (measuring external cost)
Evaluation: substitution to other unhealthy foods; obesity has many causes
Evaluation: compare with alternatives (education, regulation, nudges)
Conclusion: weigh short run vs long run; effectiveness depends on elasticity and design
levels: Precise knowledge, clear application, logical chains of reasoning, and evaluation that is balanced, using relevant context and reaching a supported judgement.
Accurate knowledge, mostly relevant application, logical chains of reasoning, appropriate evaluation with some balance.
Elements of knowledge and application; some chains of reasoning; evaluation partially developed.
Some knowledge and limited application; generic or superficial evaluation.
Isolated knowledge, little or no evaluation.
exam.tip: 25-markers split roughly 16 marks KAA and 9 marks evaluation. Aim for 3 developed KAA points and 3 evaluated counter-points, with a judgement that answers 'how effective'.

exam.q: Using a game theory matrix, explain why firms in an oligopoly might collude rather than compete on price.
points: Oligopoly: few firms, interdependence
Payoff matrix with two firms and two strategies (high price / low price)
Dominant strategy: each firm cuts price, leading to the Nash equilibrium (both low)
Both would earn more if they both kept prices high: collusion
Prisoner's dilemma explains the incentive to cheat
Collusion more likely: few firms, high barriers, similar costs, repeated games
Tacit collusion/price leadership as legal alternative; cartels illegal (CMA fines)
levels: Precise knowledge, clear application to the matrix and well-developed reasoning.
Accurate knowledge, relevant application, developed reasoning.
Some knowledge and application, limited reasoning.
Isolated knowledge.
exam.tip: Draw a clear 2x2 matrix with numbers and explain each firm's best response.

exam.q: Discuss the likely effects of a large increase in the National Living Wage on the UK labour market.
points: Minimum wage above equilibrium causes excess supply of labour (diagram)
Possible unemployment, especially in low-wage sectors (hospitality, retail)
Higher incomes reduce poverty and inequality; incentive to work
Efficiency wage theory: higher productivity and lower staff turnover
Monopsony: a minimum wage can raise both wages and employment
Evaluation: depends on elasticity of demand for labour
Evaluation: firms may substitute capital, cut hours or raise prices
Evaluation: regional differences in living costs and wages
Evaluation: evidence from the Low Pay Commission shows little job loss so far
levels: Precise knowledge, relevant application, well-developed reasoning and balanced evaluation.
Accurate knowledge and application, developed reasoning, some balanced evaluation.
Some knowledge, limited reasoning and evaluation.
Isolated knowledge.
exam.tip: Use the monopsony diagram as a strong counter-argument to the simple unemployment prediction.

exam.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of monetary policy in controlling inflation in the UK.
points: MPC sets Bank Rate to meet the 2% CPI target
Transmission mechanism: higher rates reduce consumption and investment, strengthen the pound, reduce AD
AD/AS diagram: AD shifts left, price level falls
Effective for demand-pull inflation
Evaluation: time lags of 18-24 months
Evaluation: less effective for cost-push inflation (e.g. energy prices in 2022) and may cause recession
Evaluation: depends on confidence and how many households have fixed-rate mortgages
Evaluation: conflicts with growth, unemployment, and makes government debt more expensive
Evaluation: QE and quantitative tightening as tools
Conclusion: judgement on when monetary policy works best
levels: Precise knowledge, clear application, logical chains of reasoning, balanced evaluation and supported judgement.
Accurate knowledge, relevant application, developed reasoning and some balanced evaluation.
Elements of knowledge, some reasoning, partially developed evaluation.
Some knowledge, limited reasoning, superficial evaluation.
Isolated knowledge.
exam.tip: Bring in recent UK evidence: Bank Rate rises from 0.1% in 2021 to 5.25% in 2023 and inflation peaking above 11% in October 2022.

exam.q: In an economy, the marginal propensity to save is 0.1, the marginal rate of tax is 0.2 and the marginal propensity to import is 0.2. Calculate the multiplier and the final change in national income from a £10bn increase in government spending.
points: Multiplier = 1/MPW = 1/0.5 = 2
Change in national income = 2 × £10bn = £20bn
Explanation: spending becomes income for others, who spend part of it
exam.tip: Always state the formula. Multiplier = 1/(1 − MPC) or 1/MPW.

exam.q: Assess whether supply-side policies are the best way to achieve long-term economic growth in the UK.
points: Supply-side policies shift LRAS right: potential growth without inflation
Interventionist: education and training, infrastructure (e.g. HS2), R&D
Market-based: lower taxes, deregulation, privatisation
Raise productivity, which is the main driver of long-term growth
Evaluation: long time lags; cost to the government
Evaluation: market-based policies can increase inequality
Evaluation: need demand as well; demand-side policies support growth in the short run
Judgement: most effective combined with stable demand
levels: Precise knowledge, clear application, well-developed reasoning, balanced evaluation.
Accurate knowledge, relevant application, developed reasoning.
Some knowledge and reasoning.
Isolated knowledge.
exam.tip: Use an LRAS diagram and refer to the UK productivity puzzle since 2008.

exam.q: Discuss the likely effects on the UK economy of a significant depreciation of the pound.
points: Exports cheaper, imports dearer
Current account may improve; AD rises (X − M)
Growth and employment in export industries
Imported inflation: costs for firms, higher CPI
Evaluation: Marshall-Lerner condition must hold
Evaluation: J-curve, current account worsens in the short run
Evaluation: depends on non-price competitiveness and spare capacity
Evaluation: UK imports many raw materials, so cost-push inflation may offset gains
levels: Precise knowledge, relevant application, well-developed reasoning, balanced evaluation.
Accurate knowledge, developed reasoning, some evaluation.
Some knowledge, limited reasoning.
Isolated knowledge.
exam.tip: Bring in the 2016 depreciation after the EU referendum as evidence.

exam.q: Evaluate the view that foreign direct investment is the most effective way to promote economic development in developing countries.
points: FDI brings capital, jobs, technology transfer and skills
Fills the savings gap (Harrod-Domar) and foreign currency gap
Multiplier effects and tax revenue
Evaluation: profits repatriated; transfer pricing reduces tax
Evaluation: poor working conditions and environmental damage
Evaluation: jobs may be low-skilled; MNCs may crowd out local firms
Alternative strategies: human capital, infrastructure, microfinance, fair trade, aid
Judgement: depends on institutions, regulation, and type of FDI
levels: Precise knowledge, clear application, logical chains of reasoning, balanced evaluation and supported judgement.
Accurate knowledge, developed reasoning, some balance.
Elements of knowledge, partial evaluation.
Some knowledge, superficial evaluation.
Isolated knowledge.
exam.tip: Name real countries (e.g. Vietnam, Ireland, Ethiopia) to strengthen application.

exam.q: With the help of a Lorenz curve, explain what is meant by a Gini coefficient of 0.35.
points: Lorenz curve plots cumulative % of income against cumulative % of population
45° line shows perfect equality
Gini = area between line of equality and Lorenz curve ÷ total area under line of equality
0 = perfect equality, 1 = perfect inequality
0.35 shows moderate inequality (similar to the UK)
exam.tip: Label both axes and the line of equality, and shade area A.

exam.q: Evaluate the case for nationalising the UK's water industry.
points: Water is a natural monopoly; privatised in 1989
Problems: sewage discharges (negative externalities), high debt, dividends paid to shareholders
Nationalisation could prioritise social welfare over profit, fund investment, lower prices
Evaluation: cost of buying back the firms; adds to national debt
Evaluation: state-run firms may lack incentives (X-inefficiency)
Evaluation: better regulation (Ofwat, RPI + K, fines) may be cheaper
Evaluation: government failure, political interference, short-termism
Judgement
levels: Precise knowledge, clear application, logical chains of reasoning, balanced evaluation and supported judgement.
Accurate knowledge, developed reasoning, some balance.
Elements of knowledge, partial evaluation.
Some knowledge, superficial evaluation.
Isolated knowledge.
exam.tip: Paper 3 is synoptic. Use micro (natural monopoly, regulation) and macro (public finances) together.

exam.q: The curve C has equation y = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 1. (a) Find dy/dx. (b) Find the coordinates of the stationary points of C. (c) Determine their nature.
points: M1 A1: dy/dx = 3x² − 12x + 9
M1: set 3x² − 12x + 9 = 0, so x² − 4x + 3 = 0
A1: x = 1 and x = 3, giving (1, 5) and (3, 1)
M1: d²y/dx² = 6x − 12
A1: at x = 1, −6 < 0 so maximum; at x = 3, 6 > 0 so minimum
exam.tip: Always find d²y/dx² (or check gradients either side) to justify the nature of each point.

exam.q: Use integration by parts to find ∫ x e²ˣ dx.
points: M1: u = x, dv/dx = e²ˣ, so du/dx = 1, v = ½e²ˣ
A1: uv − ∫ v du/dx dx = ½x e²ˣ − ∫ ½e²ˣ dx
M1: integrate ½e²ˣ to get ¼e²ˣ
A1: ½x e²ˣ − ¼e²ˣ
B1: + c
exam.tip: Choose u as the term that simplifies when differentiated (x here).

exam.q: (a) Express 3 cos θ + 4 sin θ in the form R cos(θ − α), where R > 0 and 0 < α < 90°. (b) Hence solve 3 cos θ + 4 sin θ = 2 for 0 ≤ θ < 360°, giving answers to 1 d.p.
exam.tip: Expand R cos(θ − α) = R cos θ cos α + R sin θ sin α and compare coefficients: R cos α = 3, R sin α = 4.

exam.q: Find the first three terms, in ascending powers of x, of the binomial expansion of (1 − 2x)^(−½), and state the range of values of x for which it is valid.
points: M1: correct structure 1 + nx + n(n − 1)x²/2 with n = −½, x replaced by −2x
B1 B1: valid for |x| < ½
exam.tip: Put brackets round (−2x) when substituting; sign errors are the most common slip.

exam.q: The value of a car, £V, t years after it was bought is modelled by V = 18000e^(−0.15t). (a) State the initial value. (b) Find the value after 4 years. (c) Find when the value first falls below £6000. (d) Give one limitation of the model.
points: A1: t = 7.32 years
B1: e.g. the value never reaches zero; other factors such as mileage and condition affect value
exam.tip: Taking ln of both sides is the key step for 'find when' questions.

exam.q: f(x) = x³ − 2x − 5. (a) Show that f(x) = 0 has a root between x = 2 and x = 3. (b) Taking x₀ = 2, apply the Newton-Raphson method once to find x₁ to 3 d.p.
points: A1: change of sign and f continuous, so a root lies in [2, 3]
exam.tip: For change of sign, you must state both values, that there is a change of sign, and that f is continuous.

exam.q: The masses of apples are normally distributed with mean 150 g and standard deviation 12 g. (a) Find the probability an apple weighs more than 165 g. (b) Find the mass m such that 10% of apples weigh less than m.
exam.tip: Calculator use is fine, but write the distribution and probability statement clearly, e.g. X ~ N(150, 12²).

exam.q: A coin is suspected of being biased towards heads. It is tossed 20 times and lands on heads 15 times. Test at the 5% level whether there is evidence the coin is biased towards heads.
points: M1: X ~ B(20, 0.5) under H₀
M1: 0.0207 < 0.05, so reject H₀
A1: there is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the coin is biased towards heads
exam.tip: Conclude in context and use non-definite language ('evidence to suggest').

exam.q: P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∪ B) = 0.7. (a) Find P(A ∩ B). (b) Find P(A | B). (c) Determine whether A and B are independent.
points: B1: P(A)P(B) = 0.2 = P(A ∩ B), so independent (or P(A|B) = P(A))
exam.tip: Show the test for independence explicitly with numbers.

exam.q: A ball is projected from ground level with speed 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², find (a) the time of flight and (b) the horizontal range.
points: M1: vertical: s = ut + ½at² with u = 20 sin 30° = 10
M1: horizontal velocity = 20 cos 30° = 17.32
exam.tip: Keep horizontal and vertical working separate and label them.

exam.q: A box of mass 5 kg is pulled along rough horizontal ground by a horizontal force of 30 N. The coefficient of friction is 0.4. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², find the acceleration of the box.
points: M1: resolve vertically: R = 5g = 49 N
M1: friction F = μR
M1: F = ma horizontally: 30 − 19.6 = 5a
exam.tip: Draw a force diagram first: weight, reaction, pull and friction.

exam.q: A uniform plank AB of length 6 m and mass 20 kg rests horizontally on supports at C and D, where AC = 1 m and DB = 2 m. A man of mass 80 kg stands on the plank at a point E. Find the largest possible distance AE for the plank to stay in equilibrium (g = 9.8 m s⁻²).
points: M1: on the point of tilting about D, reaction at C is 0
M1: take moments about D (AD = 4 m, plank's weight acts 1 m to the left of D)
A1: 20g × 1 = 80g × x, where x is the distance of E beyond D
exam.tip: 'On the point of tilting' means the reaction at the other support is zero.

exam.q: The circle C has equation x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 12 = 0. (a) Find the centre and radius of C. (b) Find the equation of the tangent to C at the point (6, 2).
points: M1: complete the square: (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 25
A1 A1: centre (3, −2), radius 5
M1: gradient of radius from (3, −2) to (6, 2) is 4/3
M1: tangent gradient −3/4
exam.tip: Tangent ⟂ radius, so the gradients multiply to −1.

exam.q: Prove that the sum of the squares of any two consecutive integers is odd.
points: M1: let the integers be n and n + 1
A1: 2(n² + n) is even, so 2(n² + n) + 1 is odd, so the statement is true
exam.tip: Finish with a clear concluding statement.

exam.q: Outline the internal working model, and explain how it may link early attachment to later relationships.
points: Internal working model: a mental template of relationships based on the first (primary) attachment
It creates expectations of how others will treat us and what we deserve
A secure early attachment leads to expectations of trusting, loving relationships later
An insecure early attachment may lead to problems such as jealousy or difficulty trusting in later relationships (e.g. Hazan and Shaver 1987)
exam.tip: 1 mark for the definition, then marks for explaining the link to childhood and adult relationships.

exam.q: Outline the English and Romanian Adoptees project and what it suggests about the effects of institutionalisation.
points: Rutter et al. followed 165 Romanian children adopted into British families, compared with 52 British adoptees
Assessed at ages 4, 6, 11, 15 and into early adulthood
Children adopted after 6 months showed disinhibited attachment
Those adopted after 6 months had lower IQ (mean 77) than those adopted before 6 months (mean 102)
Those adopted before 6 months showed few lasting differences from the controls
Suggests a sensitive period: long-term effects of institutionalisation are less likely if care improves early
exam.tip: Give the design, key findings with numbers, then a clear conclusion about institutionalisation.

exam.q: Describe and evaluate the biological approach in psychology, including the role of cognitive neuroscience.
points: AO1: behaviour has a genetic basis: genotype, phenotype, twin studies and concordance rates
AO1: evolution: behaviours that aid survival and reproduction are naturally selected
AO1: biological structures (brain areas) and neurochemistry (e.g. serotonin, dopamine) influence behaviour
AO1: cognitive neuroscience: studying how brain structures underlie mental processes using scans such as fMRI
AO3: strength: scientific, objective methods (fMRI, EEG, drug trials) give credibility
AO3: strength: real-world application, e.g. drug treatments for OCD
AO3: weakness: biologically determinist, ignores free will and the environment
AO3: weakness: correlation not causation (a chemical difference may be an effect, not a cause)
AO3: weakness: reductionist; links to the nature-nurture debate
levels: Knowledge accurate and well detailed. Discussion thorough and effective. Clear and coherent.
Knowledge evident with occasional inaccuracy. Discussion mostly effective.
Limited knowledge, some relevant. Discussion mostly ineffective.
Very limited knowledge. Discussion limited or absent.
exam.tip: Cover genes, evolution, structures and neurochemistry, and cognitive neuroscience for AO1, then build AO3 around science, determinism and causation.

exam.q: Outline and evaluate the psychodynamic approach.
points: AO1: the unconscious drives behaviour; the structure of personality: id, ego and superego
AO1: defence mechanisms: repression, denial and displacement
AO1: psychosexual stages: oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital; unresolved conflict leads to fixation
AO3: strength: explanatory power and influence on psychotherapy
AO3: weakness: concepts are unfalsifiable, so it is not scientific
AO3: weakness: based on case studies (e.g. Little Hans), hard to generalise
AO3: weakness: psychic determinism ignores free will
levels: Knowledge accurate and detailed. Evaluation clear and effective. Well organised, appropriate terminology.
Knowledge evident, occasional inaccuracy. Evaluation mostly effective.
Limited knowledge. Evaluation of limited effectiveness.
Very limited knowledge. Evaluation limited or absent.
exam.tip: Keep AO1 to the unconscious, personality, defence mechanisms and psychosexual stages; evaluate on scientific status and determinism.

exam.q: Outline and evaluate social learning theory.
points: AO1: learning through observation and imitation of role models; identification
AO1: vicarious reinforcement: seeing others rewarded makes imitation more likely
AO1: mediational processes: attention, retention, motor reproduction, motivation
AO1: Bandura et al. (1961) Bobo doll study as evidence
AO3: strength: recognises cognitive factors, unlike behaviourism
AO3: strength: real-world application, e.g. explaining cultural differences and the role of media
AO3: weakness: relies on lab studies with possible demand characteristics
AO3: weakness: underplays biological factors (e.g. testosterone and aggression)
levels: Knowledge accurate and detailed. Evaluation clear and effective. Well organised, appropriate terminology.
Knowledge evident, occasional inaccuracy. Evaluation mostly effective.
Limited knowledge, some relevant. Evaluation of limited effectiveness.
Very limited knowledge. Evaluation limited or absent.
exam.tip: Keep AO1 focused (4 marks) and give two well-developed evaluation points rather than four listed ones.

exam.q: Explain what is meant by alpha bias and beta bias. Give one example of each from psychological research.
points: Alpha bias: exaggerates differences between men and women, often devaluing women
Example of alpha bias: Freud's view that women have weaker superegos
Beta bias: ignores or minimises differences, assuming findings from men apply to women
Example of beta bias: fight or flight research on male animals applied to women (Taylor et al. 2000: tend and befriend)
Explanation of why each example fits its type of bias
Link to universality: both threaten the generality of findings
exam.tip: For each: definition, a named example, and a sentence explaining why it is that kind of bias.

exam.q: Discuss the free will versus determinism debate. Refer to examples from psychology in your answer.
points: AO1: free will: people can make their own choices; humanistic psychology
AO1: hard determinism vs soft determinism (James)
AO1: biological, environmental and psychic determinism with examples (genes, conditioning, Freud)
AO1: scientific emphasis on causal explanations
AO3: free will has face validity, and an internal locus of control is linked to better mental health (Roberts et al. 2000)
AO3: but brain activity can precede conscious decisions (Libet; Soon et al. 2008)
AO3: hard determinism conflicts with the legal system's idea of moral responsibility
AO3: determinism is unfalsifiable, as there may always be an unknown cause
AO3: soft determinism or interactionism as a middle ground; conclusion
levels: Knowledge accurate and well detailed. Discussion thorough and effective. Minor detail or expansion of argument sometimes lacking. Clear, coherent and focused, with appropriate terminology.
Knowledge evident, occasional inaccuracy. Discussion mostly effective. Mostly clear and organised, with mostly appropriate terminology.
Limited knowledge, some relevant. Discussion mostly ineffective. Lacks clarity and organisation in places.
Very limited knowledge. Discussion limited, poorly focused or absent.
exam.tip: Use examples from at least two topics (e.g. approaches, schizophrenia, attachment). Evaluate the debate, not just describe the positions.

exam.q: A psychologist recorded whether 12 participants recalled more words in a quiet room or a noisy room (repeated measures). 9 recalled more in quiet, 2 recalled more in noise and 1 recalled the same in both. Calculate the sign test value S and explain whether the result is significant at p ≤ 0.05 (critical value for N = 11 is 1).
points: Remove the participant with no difference, so N = 11
Signs: 9 of one sign and 2 of the other
S = the less frequent sign = 2
Calculated value 2 is greater than the critical value 1, so the result is not significant; accept the null hypothesis
exam.tip: With the sign test, S must be EQUAL TO OR LESS THAN the critical value to be significant. Always drop the zero differences first.

exam.q: A researcher wants to find out whether caffeine improves reaction time. Design a laboratory experiment to test this. Refer to the experimental design, the variables and how you would control extraneous variables.
points: Experimental design named and justified (e.g. independent groups to avoid order effects, or repeated measures with counterbalancing)
IV operationalised (e.g. 200 mg caffeine drink vs a decaffeinated drink that looks and tastes the same)
DV operationalised (e.g. mean reaction time in ms on a computer task over 20 trials)
Standardised procedure and instructions; same time of day, same task
Control of extraneous variables, e.g. no caffeine for 12 hours before, double-blind procedure
Sampling or ethical detail (e.g. informed consent, health screening)
exam.tip: Write it so someone else could carry it out. Every point must be applied to caffeine and reaction time, not generic.

exam.q: Explain why a pilot study might be carried out before the main study.
points: Small-scale trial run of the procedure with a few participants
Checks for problems, e.g. unclear instructions, ambiguous questions or behavioural categories, timing
Allows changes before the main study, saving time and money
exam.tip: One mark for what a pilot study is, two for clearly explained reasons.

exam.q: Prove by contradiction that there are no integers a and b such that 6a + 3b = 1.
points: B1: assume there are integers a and b with 6a + 3b = 1
M1: factorise: 3(2a + b) = 1
A1: but 2a + b is an integer (integers are closed under addition and multiplication), contradiction
A1: conclusion: so there are no integers a and b such that 6a + 3b = 1
exam.tip: Start with the word 'Assume' and end with a full conclusion that states the contradiction and the original statement.

exam.q: Prove that for all positive integers n, n³ + 2n is a multiple of 3.
points: M1: consider cases n = 3k, 3k + 1, 3k + 2 (or factorise n(n² + 2))
M1: n = 3k gives 27k³ + 6k = 3(9k³ + 2k)
A1: all cases a multiple of 3, with a concluding statement
exam.tip: Proof by exhaustion: you must cover every case. Expand carefully and show the factor of 3 explicitly.

exam.q: (a) Solve 3²ˣ − 10(3ˣ) + 9 = 0. (b) Solve log₂(x + 6) − log₂x = 2.
points: M1: (a) let y = 3ˣ: y² − 10y + 9 = 0
A1: y = 1 or y = 9
A1: x = 0 or x = 2
exam.tip: In (a) spot the hidden quadratic. In (b) combine to a single log first, then use the definition of a log to remove it.

exam.q: The mass, m grams, of a radioactive substance t days after it is measured is modelled by m = 80e^(−kt). After 5 days the mass is 60 g. (a) Find the exact value of k. (b) Find the time taken for the mass to halve, to 1 decimal place. (c) Find the rate at which the mass is decreasing when t = 10, to 2 significant figures.
points: M1: 40 = 80e^(−kt), so t = ln 2 / k
M1: dm/dt = −80k e^(−kt)
M1: substitute t = 10
A1: rate of decrease 2.6 g per day (2.58...)
exam.tip: Keep k exact until the end to avoid rounding errors. A rate of decrease is the magnitude of a negative derivative.

exam.q: A curve has equation y = x²e^(−x). (a) Find dy/dx. (b) Find the exact coordinates of the stationary points. (c) Determine the nature of each stationary point.
points: M1: product rule with u = x², v = e^(−x)
A1: dy/dx = 2xe^(−x) − x²e^(−x) = xe^(−x)(2 − x)
M1: set dy/dx = 0; e^(−x) ≠ 0
M1: find d²y/dx² = e^(−x)(x² − 4x + 2) or test the gradient either side
A1: at x = 0, d²y/dx² = 2 > 0: minimum
A1: at x = 2, d²y/dx² = −2e^(−2) < 0: maximum
exam.tip: Factorise dy/dx fully before solving, and state that e^(−x) is never 0. Exact answers means leaving e^(−2) in.

exam.q: An open box has a square base of side x cm and height h cm. Its volume is 500 cm³. (a) Show that the surface area is A = x² + 2000/x. (b) Use calculus to find the minimum surface area, justifying that it is a minimum.
points: B1: x²h = 500 so h = 500/x²
B1: A = x² + 4xh = x² + 2000/x (shown)
M1: dA/dx = 2x − 2000/x²
M1: set to 0: x³ = 1000, x = 10
A1: minimum A = 100 + 200 = 300 cm²
A1: d²A/dx² = 2 + 4000/x³ = 6 > 0 so minimum
exam.tip: For 'show that', every step must be visible. Always justify the nature of the stationary point.

exam.q: A stone is thrown from the top of a cliff 40 m above the sea, with speed 15 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. It moves freely under gravity (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). (a) Find the time taken for the stone to reach the sea. (b) Find the horizontal distance travelled. (c) Find the speed of the stone as it hits the sea. (d) State one limitation of the model.
points: M1: horizontal velocity 15 cos 30° = 12.99
A1: distance = 48.4 m
M1: vertical velocity at sea = 7.5 − 9.8t = −28.99
B1: e.g. air resistance ignored; stone treated as a particle; g assumed constant
exam.tip: Take up as positive, so the sea is at displacement −40. Solve the quadratic and reject the negative root.

exam.q: A particle is projected from a point O on horizontal ground with velocity (6i + 14.7j) m s⁻¹, where i and j are horizontal and vertical unit vectors. (a) Find the greatest height reached. (b) Find the time for which the particle is at least 7.35 m above the ground. (c) Find the angle of projection above the horizontal.
points: M1: at max height vertical velocity 0: 0 = 14.7² − 2(9.8)s
A1: greatest height 11.025 m (11.0 m)
A1: time above 7.35 m = 1.73 s (√3)
exam.tip: Two times at the same height: one going up, one coming down. The time between them is what is asked for.

exam.q: Extract A (illustrative data): The UK energy market. Six large suppliers once supplied over 90% of households. Since 2019 Ofgem has capped the price per unit that suppliers can charge households on default tariffs. When wholesale gas prices rose by over 400% in 2021-22, around 30 small suppliers left the market and the government introduced an Energy Price Guarantee, costing billions of pounds, to limit typical household bills. With reference to Extract A, explain one reason why the energy supply market might be described as an oligopoly.
points: Definition: a market dominated by a few large firms
Evidence: six large suppliers had over 90% of households (high concentration ratio)
Interdependence: firms consider rivals' prices and reactions
Other features: barriers to entry, e.g. economies of scale, wholesale price risk (30 small suppliers exited)
Brief evaluation, e.g. market concentration has changed over time or depends on definition of the market
exam.tip: Define, apply with a figure from the extract, then explain the link. Five-mark questions reward precise use of the data.

exam.q: Extract A (illustrative data): The UK energy market. Six large suppliers once supplied over 90% of households. Since 2019 Ofgem has capped the price per unit that suppliers can charge households on default tariffs. When wholesale gas prices rose by over 400% in 2021-22, around 30 small suppliers left the market and the government introduced an Energy Price Guarantee, costing billions of pounds, to limit typical household bills. Examine the likely effects of a maximum price (price cap) in the household energy market.
points: Diagram: maximum price set below equilibrium
Lower prices for households; protects consumers on low incomes (energy is a necessity, inelastic demand)
Excess demand or shortage if set below equilibrium; suppliers' profits squeezed
Firms may exit the market (link to small suppliers leaving), less competition in the long run
Reduced incentive to invest or innovate; possible fall in quality of service
Evaluation: effects depend on where the cap is set relative to costs, and how often it is reviewed
Evaluation: government failure risk (information gaps), but may correct for monopoly power
Evaluation: short run vs long run effects
levels: Accurate knowledge applied well to the context; developed chains of reasoning; relevant evaluation with a supported judgement.
Some accurate knowledge and application; some chains of reasoning; limited evaluation.
Isolated knowledge, little application to the context, little or no evaluation.
exam.tip: Use a max price diagram, apply it to energy and the extract, and give two or three evaluative points with a short judgement.

exam.q: Extract A (illustrative data): The UK energy market. Six large suppliers once supplied over 90% of households. Since 2019 Ofgem has capped the price per unit that suppliers can charge households on default tariffs. When wholesale gas prices rose by over 400% in 2021-22, around 30 small suppliers left the market and the government introduced an Energy Price Guarantee, costing billions of pounds, to limit typical household bills. Discuss the macroeconomic consequences of the government's Energy Price Guarantee.
points: Lower measured CPI inflation in the short run (energy is a large part of the CPI basket)
Supports real incomes and consumption, so AD is higher than it would have been; avoids a deeper recession
Increase in government spending and the budget deficit; higher national debt and debt interest
Possible crowding out or higher gilt yields; less fiscal space for other spending
Weakens the price signal to cut energy use; may keep demand for imported gas higher (current account effects)
Evaluation: size of multiplier and whether support was targeted (untargeted support helps high-income households too)
Evaluation: depends on time period and on whether wholesale prices fall
Evaluation: trade-off between inflation, growth and fiscal sustainability
levels: Accurate knowledge, good application to the context, developed chains of reasoning and balanced evaluation.
Some accurate knowledge and application, some reasoning, partial evaluation.
Isolated knowledge, little application or evaluation.
exam.tip: This is synoptic: link a micro intervention to macro objectives (inflation, growth, public finances). Use AD/AS reasoning.

exam.q: Extract B (illustrative data): The Bank of England raised Bank Rate from 0.1% in December 2021 to 5.25% in August 2023. CPI inflation peaked at 11.1% in October 2022 and fell to around 4% by the end of 2023. GDP growth was close to zero, unemployment rose slightly, and many households on variable-rate mortgages saw large increases in repayments. With reference to Extract B, explain how a rise in Bank Rate is expected to reduce inflation.
points: Higher interest rates raise the cost of borrowing and the reward for saving
Consumption and investment fall (e.g. higher mortgage repayments cut disposable income)
Exchange rate may appreciate, making imports cheaper and reducing AD from net exports
Lower AD reduces demand-pull inflationary pressure
Use of data: Bank Rate rose from 0.1% to 5.25% and inflation fell from 11.1% to around 4%
exam.tip: Give a clear chain from interest rates to AD to the price level, and quote figures from the extract.

exam.q: Extract B (illustrative data): The Bank of England raised Bank Rate from 0.1% in December 2021 to 5.25% in August 2023. CPI inflation peaked at 11.1% in October 2022 and fell to around 4% by the end of 2023. GDP growth was close to zero, unemployment rose slightly, and many households on variable-rate mortgages saw large increases in repayments. Assess the likely impact of higher interest rates on the UK housing market.
points: Higher mortgage costs reduce demand for houses; price falls or slower growth (demand and supply diagram)
Fewer first-time buyers can afford mortgages; affordability and deposit requirements
Higher repayments for those on variable rates reduce disposable income; some forced sales
Builders face higher financing costs, so supply of new homes may fall
Rental market: more people rent, pushing up rents
Evaluation: impact depends on the share of fixed-rate mortgages and how long rates stay high
Evaluation: housing supply is inelastic, so prices may not fall much; regional differences
Evaluation: wealth effects and confidence matter
levels: Accurate knowledge applied well to the context; developed chains of reasoning; relevant evaluation with a supported judgement.
Some accurate knowledge and application; some chains of reasoning; limited evaluation.
Isolated knowledge, little application to the context, little or no evaluation.
exam.tip: Use a supply and demand diagram for housing and bring in elasticity and time lags in evaluation.

exam.q: Extract A (illustrative data): The UK energy market. Six large suppliers once supplied over 90% of households. Since 2019 Ofgem has capped the price per unit that suppliers can charge households on default tariffs. When wholesale gas prices rose by over 400% in 2021-22, around 30 small suppliers left the market and the government introduced an Energy Price Guarantee, costing billions of pounds, to limit typical household bills. Extract B (illustrative data): The Bank of England raised Bank Rate from 0.1% in December 2021 to 5.25% in August 2023. CPI inflation peaked at 11.1% in October 2022 and fell to around 4% by the end of 2023. GDP growth was close to zero, unemployment rose slightly, and many households on variable-rate mortgages saw large increases in repayments. Evaluate whether controlling inflation should be the government's top macroeconomic priority. Refer to both extracts.
points: Costs of high inflation: falling real incomes, menu and shoe-leather costs, uncertainty reduces investment, loss of international competitiveness
Distributional effects: low-income households spend more on energy and food (link to Extract A)
Inflation expectations: if unanchored, a wage-price spiral can make it harder to control later
Trade-offs: higher interest rates slowed growth and raised unemployment risk (Extract B); short-run Phillips curve
Other objectives: growth, unemployment, balance of payments, fiscal sustainability, income distribution
Evaluation: depends on the cause of inflation (cost-push from energy prices may be temporary and less responsive to rates)
Evaluation: low and stable inflation is a precondition for sustainable growth
Evaluation: priorities change with the economic cycle and the size of the shock
Supported conclusion weighing short run vs long run
levels: Precise knowledge, clear application to the extracts, logical chains of reasoning across micro and macro, balanced evaluation and supported judgement.
Accurate knowledge, mostly relevant application, developed reasoning, appropriate evaluation with some balance.
Elements of knowledge and application, some chains of reasoning, evaluation partly developed.
Some knowledge, limited application, superficial evaluation.
Isolated knowledge, little reasoning or evaluation.
exam.tip: 25-markers on Paper 3 reward using BOTH extracts, linking micro and macro, and a final judgement that says 'it depends on...' and then decides.

exam.q: With the help of a production possibility frontier (PPF) diagram, explain the concept of opportunity cost.
points: Opportunity cost: the value of the next best alternative forgone
PPF shows the maximum combinations of two goods with given resources and technology
Correctly labelled PPF with both axes (two goods)
Movement along the PPF: producing more of one good means producing less of the other
Concave shape shows increasing opportunity cost, as resources are not equally suited to both goods
exam.tip: Label both axes with named goods and mark two points on the curve so the trade-off is visible.

exam.q: A country's Consumer Prices Index (CPI) rose from 130.0 to 135.2 over one year. Calculate the rate of inflation, and explain one limitation of the CPI as a measure of changes in the cost of living.
points: Limitation identified, e.g. CPI excludes mortgage interest payments and council tax
Explained: households with large mortgages may face a higher rise in living costs than CPI shows
Alternative: basket is an average, so it misses spending patterns of particular groups (e.g. pensioners)
exam.tip: Show the formula with numbers in it before the answer; the limitation must say why it matters for some households.

exam.q: Examine the likely effects of a fall in consumer confidence on aggregate demand in the UK.
points: Consumption is the largest component of AD (around 60% in the UK)
Lower confidence raises the saving ratio, so consumption falls
AD shifts left: lower real GDP and downward pressure on the price level
Multiplier effect makes the final fall in GDP larger than the initial fall in spending
Firms may also delay investment if they expect weaker demand
Evaluation: size depends on the marginal propensity to consume, interest rates and wealth effects
Evaluation: offsetting factors, e.g. a Bank Rate cut or a weaker pound boosting net exports
exam.tip: Examine means analyse and weigh up: give the chain of reasoning, then at least one point that limits or offsets the effect.

exam.q: Using an AD/AS diagram, assess the likely impact of a sharp rise in global energy prices on the UK economy.
points: Energy is a key input, so costs of production rise across the economy
SRAS shifts left on the AD/AS diagram
Cost-push inflation: higher price level
Lower real GDP and possible rise in unemployment (stagflation)
Real incomes fall, which can also reduce AD
Evaluation: impact depends on how long the price rise lasts and on energy intensity of UK firms
Evaluation: government support (e.g. price caps) or Bank of England response changes the outcome
levels: Precise knowledge, clear application to the context and a balanced, well-supported judgement.
Accurate knowledge, relevant application, developed analysis with some evaluation.
Some knowledge and application, limited analysis.
Isolated knowledge.
exam.tip: Draw SRAS shifting left with the new price level and real GDP marked, then judge how large and lasting the effect is.

exam.q: Evaluate the view that the benefits of economic growth always outweigh its costs.
points: Benefits: higher incomes and living standards (real GDP per capita)
Benefits: more tax revenue for public services without higher tax rates; lower unemployment
Costs: environmental damage and depletion of resources (negative externalities)
Costs: inequality may widen if gains go mainly to high earners
Costs: demand-pull inflation and current account deficit if growth exceeds trend
Evaluation: sustainable vs unsustainable growth; type and source of growth matter
Evaluation: depends on stage of development and how gains are distributed; judgement reached
levels: Precise knowledge, application throughout, developed chains of reasoning and a supported overall judgement.
Accurate knowledge and application, developed analysis, evaluation that weighs factors.
Some relevant knowledge and application, partial analysis, limited evaluation.
Isolated knowledge, little application.
exam.tip: The word always is the hook: your conclusion should say when benefits outweigh costs and when they do not.

exam.q: Explain two reasons why many firms remain small.
points: Reason 1 identified, e.g. small market size or niche market
Reason 1 explained with economic reasoning (e.g. limited demand means no scope for economies of scale)
Reason 2 identified, e.g. owner objectives (lifestyle, keeping control)
Reason 2 explained (e.g. growth would need outside investors and loss of control)
Other valid reasons: lack of finance, diseconomies of scale, personalised service
exam.tip: Two reasons, each with a because: identify, then explain the economics behind it.

exam.q: A firm sells 400 units a week at £12 each. Its total costs are £3,600 a week, of which £1,200 are fixed costs. Calculate the firm's weekly profit and its average variable cost, and explain whether it should keep producing in the short run if the price fell to £5.
points: Total revenue = 400 × £12 = £4,800
Short-run shutdown rule: produce only if price ≥ AVC
At £5, price < AVC (£6), so the firm should shut down in the short run
exam.tip: State the shutdown rule (P ≥ AVC) and compare the new price to your AVC figure.

exam.q: Explain why a firm might aim to maximise sales revenue rather than profit.
points: Profit maximisation at MC = MR; revenue maximisation at MR = 0
Diagram: revenue-maximising output is higher and price lower than profit-maximising output
Divorce of ownership and control: principal-agent problem
Managers' pay and status may be linked to revenue or firm size rather than profit
Higher revenue can build market share and economies of scale for later profit
Lower prices may deter entry or win customers in a competitive market
Shareholders may accept this if a satisfactory level of profit is still made (satisficing)
exam.tip: Show both outputs on one diagram with MR = 0 and MC = MR clearly marked.

exam.q: Assess the importance of the Bank of England acting as lender of last resort to commercial banks.
points: Lender of last resort: lends to banks that cannot raise funds elsewhere
Prevents liquidity problems turning into bank runs and failures
Protects the payment system and confidence in the financial system (systemic risk)
Example: support for banks during the 2007-08 financial crisis
Evaluation: moral hazard, as banks may take bigger risks expecting a rescue
Evaluation: regulation (capital and liquidity requirements) reduces how often it is needed
Judgement on overall importance
levels: Precise knowledge, clear application to the context and a balanced, well-supported judgement.
Accurate knowledge, relevant application, developed analysis with some evaluation.
Some knowledge and application, limited analysis.
Isolated knowledge.
exam.tip: Use a real example, and balance stability against moral hazard before giving a judgement.

exam.q: f(x) = 2x³ − 5x² − 4x + 3. (a) Use the factor theorem to show that (x − 3) is a factor of f(x). (b) Hence factorise f(x) completely.
points: M1: divide to get f(x) = (x − 3)(2x² + x − 1)
M1: factorise the quadratic
exam.tip: For "show that", write the conclusion: f(3) = 0, so (x − 3) is a factor.

exam.q: (a) Express (5x + 1)/((x + 1)(x − 1)) in partial fractions. (b) Hence find the exact value of ∫ from 2 to 3 of (5x + 1)/((x + 1)(x − 1)) dx, giving your answer as a single logarithm.
points: M1: integrate to 2ln(x + 1) + 3ln(x − 1)
M1: substitute limits: (2ln 4 + 3ln 2) − (2ln 3 + 3ln 1)
M1: combine using log laws: 7ln 2 − 2ln 3
exam.tip: Substituting the roots of each bracket is the fastest way to find A and B.

exam.q: The points A and B have position vectors 2i − j + 3k and 5i + 3j + 3k. (a) Find |AB|. (b) Find a unit vector in the direction of AB. (c) Find the angle between AB and the vector i, to 1 decimal place.
points: M1: AB = b − a = 3i + 4j + 0k
A1: unit vector = (3/5)i + (4/5)j
M1: cos θ = 3/5
exam.tip: AB is b − a, not a − b; check the sign before finding the magnitude.

exam.q: Explain the difference between stratified sampling and quota sampling, and give one advantage of each.
points: B1: stratified sampling selects randomly from each stratum, in proportion to its size
B1: quota sampling fills a set number from each group, chosen by the interviewer (not random)
B1: advantage of stratified, e.g. sample reflects population structure and is random so less biased
B1: advantage of quota, e.g. no sampling frame needed, quick and cheap
exam.tip: The key difference examiners look for: stratified is random within groups, quota is not.

exam.q: For a sample of 20 daily rainfall readings, Σx = 360 and Σx² = 6800. (a) Find the mean and standard deviation. (b) An outlier is defined as a value more than 2 standard deviations from the mean. Is a reading of 27 an outlier? Show your reasoning.
points: M1: variance = 6800 ÷ 20 − 18²
A1: = 340 − 324 = 16, so standard deviation = 4
M1: upper limit = 18 + 2 × 4 = 26
A1: 27 > 26, so 27 is an outlier
exam.tip: Variance is "mean of the squares minus square of the mean"; remember to square-root for the standard deviation.

exam.q: Solve, for 0° ≤ x < 360°, the equation 2cos²x + 3sin x = 3.
points: M1: use cos²x = 1 − sin²x
M1: 2 − 2sin²x + 3sin x = 3, so 2sin²x − 3sin x + 1 = 0
M1: factorise (2sin x − 1)(sin x − 1) = 0
A1: sin x = 1/2 or sin x = 1
exam.tip: Turn everything into one trig function first, then solve the quadratic; find every solution in the range.

exam.q: Find the exact area of the region enclosed between the curves y = x² and y = 4x − x².
points: M1: set x² = 4x − x², so 2x² − 4x = 0
A1: x = 0 and x = 2
M1: area = ∫ from 0 to 2 of (4x − x² − x²) dx = ∫ (4x − 2x²) dx
M1: integrate to 2x² − (2/3)x³
M1: substitute limits: 8 − 16/3
A1: area = 8/3
exam.tip: Subtract the lower curve from the upper curve inside one integral.

exam.q: An arithmetic series has first term 7 and common difference 4. Find the least number of terms needed for the sum to exceed 1000.
points: M1: set 2n² + 5n − 1000 > 0 and solve 2n² + 5n − 1000 = 0
M1: check: S₂₁ = 987, S₂₂ = 1078
A1: least n = 22
exam.tip: Round up, not to the nearest whole number, and check the neighbouring values.

exam.q: The circle C has equation x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 12 = 0. (a) Find the centre and radius of C. (b) Show that the point P(6, 2) lies on C. (c) Find the equation of the tangent to C at P, in the form ax + by + c = 0.
points: M1: complete the square: (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 25
A1: centre (3, −2), radius 5
M1: gradient of radius = (2 − (−2)) ÷ (6 − 3) = 4/3
M1: tangent gradient = −3/4
exam.tip: The tangent is perpendicular to the radius at that point: gradients multiply to −1.
